Ruleborn

Game design document, version 2.3

Collect the laws of nature, build a universe that runs on them, and pull off heists in universes that run on someone else's.

This document defines the whole game from moment zero: its scope, every system, and the logic that connects them. Names and numbers are starting values, written to be tuned.

Draft for review, September 2026. Native iPhone game built in Godot 4.5, rated 13+, for players aged 16 to 34 at its core; iPhone and Android together at global launch.

What changed in version 2.3

A naming and compliance pass over the whole document, on the assumption that no trade mark will be filed.

  • The game is now Ruleborn. No game called Lawbound existed, but "-bound" is crowded in the classes that matter — Stormbound and Bladebound are both registered for game software — and unregistered rights only cover the market actually used. Ruleborn is coined, sits in a far emptier field, and names the creatures rather than the constraint, which is the better story: the game is named for what was born from the scattered laws (26.9).
  • The lawborn are the ruleborn. One word for the creatures and the game, the way the best collection games do it.
  • Four other names changed. The Echo Knight became the Echoplate — it shared both the name and the mechanic of a well-known tabletop subclass. The Moss Giant became the Mossbear. Masquerade became Borrowed Face, which describes the law better anyway. The Creator Fund became the Island Fund.
  • Everything else stands: the realms, the notes, the schools and the rest of the creatures are either coined or ordinary words used ordinarily.
  • The asset ledger has its first entries (21.11): both typefaces, open-licensed for embedding, with the licence text shipped in settings.
  • This is a check against what is findable, not a legal clearance. The register search still happens before anything is public.

1Vision, pillars and audience

Ruleborn is a strategy game about floating islands that each follow a magic rule. On one island stones float, on another rivers crawl, on a third anyone knocked down comes back as an echo. You collect these rules, build your islands around them, and send a small crew of odd little creatures to rob other players' islands by outsmarting theirs.

1.1 The pitch

Where it's usedLine
Store and trailerYour islands. Your rules. Their treasure.
One sentence for a friend"I build floating islands with their own magic rules, and I rob other people's islands by outsmarting theirs."
For the teamPikmin-style crews pulling heists through Monument Valley-style islands that players design and share, with Balatro-style combinations of rules and a Pokémon-style collection of creatures shaped by those rules (see 2).

1.2 The seven pillars

Every feature has to serve at least one of these. When two ideas compete, the one that serves more pillars wins.

PillarWhat it means in practice
Every rule changes the gameA new law changes how the game plays, not just its numbers, and you can see it in how everything moves. Adding one law creates hundreds of new situations.
Clever beats strongHeists are won by reading an island's rules and finding a way through, not by bigger stats.
Your islands are yours, and anyone can play themWhich islands you open, how you shape them, which rules you write into them and which creatures you raise make every player's sky different, and the Island Workshop lets anyone publish an island for everyone to play (18.6).
Better with friendsFriends raid together, gift to each other, trade creatures and see each other's best moments. The strongest predictor of staying with a game is having people to play with (19.9).
Nothing is wastedCharacters are never spent, failure returns them tired rather than lost, losses are capped, and defending well pays.
Short sessions, deep planningA session is 5 to 9 minutes. The depth lives in planning, which can happen away from the screen.
Worth your timePlayers come back because they want to, not because they have to (see 19).

1.3 Audience

The core audience is players aged 16 to 34, with 25 to 34 at its heart: people who enjoy clever puzzles, strategy and collecting, and who are tired of pay-to-win and endless timers. Older players are welcome. The game is rated 13+, is not made for or marketed to children, and gives players aged 13 to 17 extra protections (see 20).

1.4 How we talk about it

The fiction is a storybook, not a science lesson. Words players see are plain and warm.

We sayWe don't say
Island, rule, law, page, crew, vault, heist, skiff, KeeperPhysics, code, algorithm, simulation, dimension, hacking
"This island's rule: stones float""Gravity coefficient reduced by 50%"
"Your crew got away with 3,200 Starlight""Extraction successful; yield 3,200"

1.5 The ambition

The goal is a game that could become one of the most successful ever made. No honest analysis can promise or estimate that before launch: in 2025 only nine mobile games passed $1 billion in player spending, and strong launches still fail (2.7). So the ambition becomes three commitments:

  • Design toward what the record holders share (2.6), without copying their weaknesses.
  • Set gates at the level of the top 1% of games at every stage (25.1). Only a game that clears them has earned a mega-hit forecast.
  • Change course when the evidence says no, rather than scaling a game that isn't working.

2Lessons from the most successful games

Version 0.1 leaned on Clash of Clans and Clash Royale. This section widens the lens to the biggest earners, the most downloaded, and the most loved games of 2024 to 2026, and turns each into something Ruleborn takes or avoids.

2.1 What the charts say

  • In 2025 the top-grossing mobile games were live-service titles driven by events and collaborations: MONOPOLY GO!, Royal Match, Whiteout Survival, Last War and Honor of Kings traded the top spots month by month [26].
  • The most downloaded were the lowest-friction: Block Blast! held the top spot for much of 2025, alongside Roblox, Free Fire and Subway Surfers [26].
  • The biggest new hit was a collection game: Pokémon TCG Pocket made an estimated $1.3 billion in its first year and passed 150 million downloads, built on two free packs a day, showcases and trading [27].
  • Premium and indie games proved depth sells on phones too: Balatro passed 5 million copies [28], and Stardew Valley passed 41 million [29].
  • And a warning: Supercell ended development of Squad Busters in October 2025. It was the studio's first new global game since Brawl Stars, and after several reworks it became the first global game Supercell has ever shut down [30].

2.4 What changed because of this

  • A diorama camera you can rotate, instead of the fixed three-quarter view every base builder uses (21.1).
  • Combinations are the core of discovery through notes, harmonies and chords (8).
  • Pikmin-like crews with telegraphed enemies make heists about reading and timing (12.6 to 12.8).
  • Collection and showing off: Codex albums, island showcases and page trading.
  • Player-made islands become content through weekly defence challenges.
  • No base destruction and no wars: heists, co-op and friendly leagues.

2.7 The honest odds

  • In 2025 only 9 mobile games passed $1 billion in player spending and 828 passed $10 million, while the top 1% of publishers took 92.5% of in-app revenue [36].
  • Even a strong launch from the best studio can fail, as Squad Busters did [30], and soft-launch numbers can fade.
  • Scale in plain arithmetic: earning $2 billion a year means about $5.5 million a day. That is 18 million daily players spending 30 cents each, or 37 million spending 15 cents. Cosmetic-only games are likely nearer the lower figure, an assumption to test. With a third of monthly players playing on a given day, that means 60 to 120 million monthly players.
  • So the forecast is earned, not assumed: the gates in 25.1 say what would have to be true at each stage.

3Setting and tone

Long ago, an old keeper called the Archivist looked after the Book of Laws, a huge book whose pages told the world how to behave: stones fall, rivers flow, echoes fade. One stormy night the Book burst open. Its pages scattered across the sky, and wherever a page came to rest, a small island lifted into the air and began to follow what was written on it.

Now the sky is full of islands with strange little rules. Keepers are the people who look after a cluster of them. They gather torn pages of the Book, restore them, and write the laws into their own islands, which makes them richer and more wonderful. Other Keepers' islands hold pages you've never seen, and treasure worth borrowing.

In the storyIn the game
A page of the Book of LawsA law. Collecting enough torn pages of a law restores it.
A floating islandA realm. Each follows the laws written into it.
A Keeper's cluster of islandsThe player's universe: the Heart and up to six outer realms.
The little creatures born on the islandsRuleborn, shaped by the laws of the island where they hatch.
The Archivist and other wise old keepersSages, the heroes who can bend a rule for a moment.
The skiffThe small flying boat a crew uses to land on and leave another Keeper's islands.
  • Tone: wonder, cleverness and warmth; a heist caper in a picture-book sky. Nothing is killed; knocked-out characters wake up at home.
  • Look: floating island dioramas under a violet sky; each school of law has its own colour and shape; every law visible in how the world and its creatures move (see 21).
  • Humour: gentle and physical. Creatures slip on frictionless ground, sleepwalking guards bump into trees, and puffballs bleat at the worst moment.

The Archivist's laws are also called the rules of the world, and the creatures born where a page landed are the ruleborn. Both words mean the same thing; Keepers use whichever the moment calls for.

4Core loops

Ruleborn has four loops nested inside each other. The inner loops happen every session; the outer loops give reasons to come back for months.

  1. Heists
  2. Loot, pages, renown, strays
  3. New laws, buildings, realms, discoveries
  4. Stronger characters, cleverer defence

Then back to better heists. Each turn around the loop takes one or two sessions early on and a few days later.

LoopLengthWhat the player doesWhat it feeds
Heist3 minutesScout, plan a route, cross realms, open the vault, escapeLoot, pages, renown
Session5 to 9 minutesCollect production, reassign workers, run one or two heists, weave or upgrade, queue a Lab experimentSteady growth and a reason to return in an hour
Discovery2 to 5 daysUnlock a law from pages, open a realm, find a resonance, redesign the mapNew ways to play and defend
Season8 weeksClimb renown leagues, fight anomalies with the constellation, adapt to weekly eras, optionally begin a new epochLong-term goals and fresh starts
Logic

The two scarce things are stability (how much law your universe can hold) and characters' time (each one can work, guard or raid, never two at once). Almost every decision in the game is a choice about one of these two.

5Your universe

A Keeper's universe is a small sky of floating islands: the Heart and up to six outer realms, joined by bridges. This section sets out where each kind of rule applies, how realms and links work, how raiders arrive, and how much law a universe can hold.

5.1 Where rules apply

Rules nest like boxes. Each box sits inside a bigger one, and when rules meet, the smaller, inner box has the final say.

ScopeSet byApplies toLastsExample
EraThe gameEvery universeOne weekHigh Tide: Slow rivers costs no stability
Grand LawA constellation's voteEvery member's universe, as a free extra crown lawOne weekBloom in every member's realms
Crown lawThe Keeper, at the SpireEvery realm of that universe, at full strengthWhile wovenStillness everywhere: raiders can hide in any realm, but so can nothing move unseen
Realm lawThe Keeper, at the SpireOne realm onlyWhile wovenSlow rivers in Tidehold
TerrainThe KeeperThe tiles it coversUntil changedA pond, tall grass, a cliff
ZoneWards, raider casts, Sage powersA circle of tilesSecondsA cast of Haste for 10 seconds
CharacterBirth, traits, levelOne character, everywhereAlwaysA Swimmer ignores Slow rivers
Logic: crown and realm laws
  • A crown law works in every realm of its universe, including the Heart, and costs double stability. The Spire opens 1 crown slot at Spire level 2 and a second at Spire level 5.
  • A realm law works only in its own realm. The Heart has 2 realm slots; outer realms have 1, 2 or 3 by realm level.
  • The same law can't be both a crown law and a realm law in one universe; the stronger tier would simply apply.
  • A crown law adds 5% to its school's resource in every realm; a realm law adds 10% in its own realm.

5.2 Realms

Every universe has one Heart and up to six outer realms. Outer realms open at Keeper levels 3, 6, 10, 15, 21 and 28, and the player picks each one's type from those not yet owned, so a finished universe has one realm of each type.

5.3 Links

LinkCrossingSpecial ruleLimitCost
Stone bridgeNormal speedCan hold one wardNoneFree
Rope bridge30% fasterCan carry a Snap that drops the bridge; anyone on it falls backNone300
ChuteFast, one wayThe owner sets the direction21,500

  • The Heart has four link sockets and outer realms three. Every realm must connect to the Heart.
  • A universe needs one link per outer realm and may have two extra, for loops and shortcuts.
  • At least one walkable route must reach the Heart from every outer realm's edge. The game refuses layouts that seal the Vault.

5.4 Landing and leaving

Raiders arrive by skiff, a small flying boat, and the whole edge of the universe is open to them. Defenders can't choose where raiders come from; they can only make every edge a puzzle.

RuleDetail
LandingThe crew lands on any edge tile of any outer realm the raider chooses. The Heart is ringed by strong winds, so skiffs can't land there.
Being seen landingA landing skiff can be heard: guards within 6 tiles of the landing spot start at 25% awareness, unless the spot is in fog, darkness or tall grass.
LeavingAt any time the crew can call the skiff to any edge tile of any realm. It takes 5 seconds to reach an outer realm and 20 seconds to fight the winds around the Heart. The crew must hold the spot until it arrives.
FaultsWhen a universe is overloaded (5.5), faults open between realms: cracks a crew can jump through once per heist, ignoring the links.
Heist clock150 seconds plus 15 seconds for each link on the shortest route from the landing realm to the Heart, up to 240 seconds.
Why open landing

Choosing where to land is one of the most fun decisions a raider makes, and it shouldn't belong to the defender. Open edges also make defence about the whole island: cliffs, tall grass, lantern light and laws along every edge, not one guarded gate.

5.5 Stability

Stability is how much law a universe can hold. It now comes from buildings, so growing it is part of the economy, and its effects come in seven bands instead of three.

Capacity = Keeper's Spire (30 + 8 × Spire level) + every Anchor Stone (8 + 5 × its level), raised 8% for each epoch after the first
Cost of a law = base cost × tier (1.0, 1.3 or 1.6) × 2 if crowned × 0.8 in a realm of its school × 0.85 for each harmony × 0.8 for a signature resonance × 0.9 in a chord × 1.25 for a dissonance
Strain = total cost of woven laws ÷ capacity

Harmonies, resonances, chords and dissonances come from the notes laws carry (see 8). At the maximum, a Spire at level 10 and seven Anchor Stones at level 10 give 516 stability, while a full set of 22 woven laws at tier III costs around 500 to 560, so a finished universe always sits near its limit.

BandStrainEffectWhat the islands look like
QuietUnder 40%NoneStill air; laws barely visible
Steady40 to 70%+5% production everywherePylons glow softly
Humming70 to 90%+10% productionA low hum; motes drift up from the pylons
Brimming90 to 100%+15% production; pylons have 10% more healthIslands shimmer; the Spire's rings spin faster
Strained100 to 110%+15% production; one fault opens between two realmsA glowing crack runs across one island
Cracking110 to 125%Two or three faults; during heists each law has a 5% chance every 10 seconds of blinking off for 2 secondsCracks spread; laws flicker
Breaking125% and overNo new weaving; four faults; laws flicker twice as oftenIslands tremble; stones drift loose
Logic

Production bonuses reward using the capacity you've built; faults and flickering are the price of pushing past it. Overloading is a legitimate choice for a player who wants more laws and accepts a weaker defence. Faults close as soon as strain drops back under 100%.

5.6 Weaving laws

  • Laws are woven into slots at the Keeper's Spire: 10 minutes at tier I, 40 minutes at tier II and 2 hours at tier III. Weaving costs 40 Aether per point of the law's stability cost.
  • While a slot is being woven it is empty. Removing a law is instant, but the slot then rests for an hour before it can be woven again.
  • Upkeep is 0.5 Aether an hour per point of cost. It pauses once the player has been away for 24 hours, and if Aether runs out, laws run at half strength rather than switching off.

5.7 The realm bible

Each realm type has a palette, a soundtrack, wildlife, a level-design pattern that shapes how heists play there, and one signature moment it exists to produce. The pattern is the important part: it is what makes a Tidehold heist feel different from an Emberreach heist even before any law is woven.

6Terrain

Without walls, the ground shapes every route. Terrain is the Keeper's main building material for defence: 39 features in seven families, each changing how creatures move, what guards can see, and how laws behave.

6.1 Rules

  • Budget: an outer realm has 30 terrain points plus 15 per realm level (45 to 105). The Heart has 40 plus 10 per Spire level. Reshaping is free and instant; it's the budget that limits it.
  • Snapshots: a heist is played against the terrain as it was when the heist started.
  • The route rule: terrain can lengthen routes but never close the last route from the edges to the Heart.
  • Height: four heights (0 to 3). Dropping down is free and one-way, so height creates one-way paths without chutes.
  • Noise: stairs, gravel, scree, bells and bounce mushrooms make noise; noise raises the awareness of guards nearby.

Why so much terrain

Terrain is cheap to build in code, readable at a glance, and multiplies with laws: 39 features against 48 laws give well over a thousand distinct interactions, most of them visible in how creatures move. It also makes defence creative, which is what feeds the weekly defence challenges (18.5).

7Laws

Laws are the torn pages of the Book: rules an island follows. They are what players collect, the source of each island's economy and defence, and the puzzle in every heist. There are 48 at launch in six schools, three paradoxes found only in the Lab, and a system of notes that decides how laws combine (see 8).

7.1 What a law is

PropertyRule
SchoolOne of six families, each with a colour and a shape so it never depends on colour alone.
RankCommon, uncommon, rare or deep, with paradoxes outside the scale. Rank sets how long a law takes to acquire — not how strong it is (7.10).
Stability costFrom 10 to 26 points (40 to 50 for paradoxes), before the modifiers in 5.5.
NotesOne or two of eight notes (Flow, Weight, Glow, Hush, Bloom, Echo, Spark, Veil) that decide harmonies and dissonances (8).
TiersI, II and III. Higher tiers are stronger and cost more stability (× 1.3 and × 1.6).
Where it appliesAs a realm law, in one realm; as a crown law, in every realm of the universe (5.1).
SymmetryA law applies to everyone where it rules: the owner's guards and wards as much as a raiding crew.
Movement signatureEvery law changes how characters move, so a player can read the rule by watching (7.4, 21.7).
EconomyA realm law adds 10% to its school's resource in its realm; a crown law adds 5% everywhere.

7.2 Schools

SchoolShapeThemeBoostsMost common notes

MatterCubeWalls, weight, glass, crystalStarlightWeight, Glow

7.3 How laws combine

Each realm has a rule sheet of parameters that every character, guard and ward reads. Laws change parameters; they never contain special cases for particular characters.

ParameterDefaultChanged by, for example
Speed and direction1.0 ×, freeHaste, Current, Tilt, Inward pull, Wild paths, Honeycomb
Jumping, climbing, leaping1 tile, no climbingHalf gravity, Heavy ground, Leapfrog, Honeycomb
FrictionOnFrictionless, ice
Sight, light and hearing6 tiles, light, normal hearingGlowing dark, Aurora, Day and night, Glass, Sleepwalk
Trails and noiseNoneSpark trails, Haunting, Afterimage, Leapfrog, Flock
Damage and toughness1.0 ×Brittle stone, Heat bloom, Density
Healing and regrowthNoneRegrowth, Kinship, Bloom
Flow of timeConstantHaste, Delay, Rewind, Held breath
Loot weight and type1.0 ×, fixedHeavy ground, Transmute, Lodestones
Who is whoClearMirror images, Borrowed Face
RevivalNoneEchoes, Soul swap, Swarm birth
Logic: order of application
  1. Start from the defaults.
  2. Apply the Era, then the Grand Law, then crown laws, then the realm's laws, in the fixed school order Motion, Matter, Time, Energy, Life, Spirit.
  3. Apply terrain, then zones (wards and raider casts).
  4. Apply Sage powers, which can suspend or flip any law.
  5. Apply each character's own traits and immunities last.

Multipliers multiply; on/off rules take the last value applied. The simulation runs at a fixed 20 steps a second so heists replay identically on the server.

7.5 Paradoxes

Paradoxes are wild laws found only in the Lab, by combining two tier III laws with opposite notes. Each such experiment has a 10% chance of revealing one, and the Lab warns when a pairing is "unstable". A universe can hold one paradox at a time, and paradoxes give no economy bonus.

ParadoxCostEffectHow characters move
Reversal45The Heart swaps places with the outermost realm: the Vault moves to the frontier and every route is reversed.Everyone walks with a slight upside-down sway; hair points at the sky.
Twin suns50Every other law in the realm applies twice.Every character casts two shadows and moves with doubled flourishes.
Unmaking40Every 20 seconds one law in the realm, raider casts included, switches off at random for 10 seconds.Characters stutter as rules blink in and out.

7.6 Getting and improving laws

  • Pages from heists, which is the point of raiding. After each heist the player picks one law the crew crossed to study and receives 2 of its pages, 3 if the heist was clean. The first time a player meets a law it joins the Codex with 1 page. Breaking a pylon gives a page of its law; a foiled heist gives one.
  • Raiding is the efficient path, not the only one. A Library at the Heart produces about one page per realm every few hours — enough to keep restoring something slowly, nowhere near enough to raise a school. A single heist is worth roughly two to three sessions of that trickle. Making raiding the sole source would punish the many players who prefer building (13.1), and gating a resource behind one activity is where players stop feeling directed and start feeling forced [210].
  • Pages lean toward what you raided. Raiding a Tidehold yields mostly Time pages — around two in three — with the rest spread across the schools you met. That is enough to make "I want Time laws, so I raid Tideholds" a real plan, without the resentment that comes from an exclusive lock [211].
  • Nothing is gated by the clock. No day-of-the-week rotations, no timed schools, no windows. The most-complained-about version of directional farming is the one that decides when you may pursue what you want [210]; ours decides only where.
  • A floor for bad luck. Every eighth heist guarantees a page of a law you are actually working on, so an unlucky run of targets never costs a week.
  • The Codex opens in chapters: 12 laws are findable from the start, 24 from Keeper level 6, 36 from level 12, 42 from level 18, and all 48 from level 24. Matchmaking only shows universes running laws from open chapters.
  • Restoring a law: 15 pages for a common law, 30 for a rare one, 60 for a deep one.
  • Tiers: tier II costs 20 more pages and 2,000 Aether (Spire level 4); tier III costs 40 more pages and 8,000 Aether (Spire level 7).
  • Other sources: Lab experiments that find nothing give 3 pages of a law from those schools; the Collector swaps pages; constellation members can gift pages; daily goals give a few.
  • Starting laws: Half gravity, Slow rivers and Bloom, all at tier I.
Why pages come from crossing

Players learn new laws by experiencing them on someone else's island. Every heist is also a lesson, which gives a reason to raid islands with unfamiliar laws rather than always the easiest target.

7.9 How much there is to understand

Depth comes from combining laws, which is also the biggest risk: too many unfamiliar rules at once and new players leave. Every heist has a complexity budget.

RuleKeeper levels 1 to 910 to 1920 and up
Laws on the route the player has never met1 at most2 at most3 at most
Rules that interact at any one momentNever more than 4, at any level. Working memory holds about four chunks of new, interacting information [75] [76], and difficulty rises with how many pieces must be held at once [77] [78]. A realm may hold more laws than that only when the extra ones do not interact with the crew's route.
Realms on a typical route2 to 33 to 43 to 5
Harmony shown on the routeHarmonies onlyPlus signature resonancesPlus chords and paradoxes
  • Laws are always visible: every law has a movement signature, a world signature, a card with a looping preview, and a two-second banner when the crew enters its realm.
  • Colour is never the only signal: every school has a shape, and every note has a small symbol.
  • Each law is taught alone first: the Drifting ruins introduce each new law on its own before it appears in combinations (15).

7.10 Rarity buys specificity, not strength

Version 2.0 splits three ranks into four, plus paradoxes. The rule behind the split matters more than the split: rarity governs how long a law takes to get, while stability cost and conditions govern how strong it is. These are two dials, and the earlier version tied them together.

RankCountCharacterPages to restore
Common18Always useful, small effect, no drawback. Three per school10
Uncommon14Conditional, with a mild cost20
Rare10Strong inside a condition you have to build for35
Deep6Changes how a realm works. Heavy stability cost and a real trade-off. One per school60
Paradox3Universe-wide, one at a time, found only in the Lab120

This follows the published design philosophy of the game that invented collectable rarity: rarity is set by complexity, size of effect and excitement, and a higher rarity does not mean a card must be more powerful [207]. The honest counter-evidence is that in every large shipped game rarer cards are stronger in practice, and no competitive game has fully achieved the separation [208]. So something else has to do the balancing work.

Power is paid for with legibility

A deep law is more dramatic, not more efficient — and every rare and deep law appears in the scout report (12.5). Raiders can see it coming and plan around it. This visibility is charged against the law's strength the way range is charged against a character's kit, and it is the primary reason a rare law can be exciting without being unfair. If playtests show rare and deep laws still producing materially higher defence rates than common ones, the answer is more stability cost or a tighter condition, not a smaller number.

  • Conditions, not punishments. A rare law is powerful when a condition you control is met. Laws that simply hurt their owner are avoided: the evidence on collectable design is that conditional build-around power is enjoyed while flat drawbacks are resented [207].
  • Collecting is grouped by school, eight laws each. A set of 48 is far past the point where a collection reads as completable, while seven to twelve is where people push to finish [209]; six sets of eight gives that feeling six times over.

8Harmony: how laws combine

Version 0.2 had a list of 32 special pairs. Harmony replaces that with a system players can learn and predict: every law carries one or two notes, and notes decide what happens when laws share an island. Players meet it like music: some laws sound well together, some clash, and a few special combinations sing.

8.1 The eight notes

NoteWhat laws with this note doOppositeSymbol
FlowChange how things move: speed, direction, jumping, slidingWeightA wave
WeightSlow, pull, hold and weigh downFlowAn anchor
GlowLight, reveal and showHushA sun
HushHide, silence and stillGlowA crescent
BloomGrow, heal and multiplySparkA sprout
SparkBurst, stun, break and surgeBloomA star
EchoReturn, repeat and rewindVeilA ring
VeilDisguise, deceive and transformEchoA mask

8.2 Harmonies

When two laws in the same realm share a note, they harmonise. Crown laws count in every realm, so a crown law can harmonise with every realm's laws. A harmony lowers the stability cost of both laws by 15% and strengthens the shared kind of effect. Harmonies are shown automatically when weaving, so players learn them by doing.

Shared noteHarmony effect on both lawsExample
FlowMovement effects 25% strongerCurrent + Tilt: wind and slope together
WeightSlowing and pulling 25% strongerSlow rivers + Heavy ground
GlowLight and reveal ranges 2 tiles longerSoul lanterns + Spark trails
HushHiding works 1 tile closer to guardsStillness + Glowing dark
BloomRegrowth and healing 25% strongerBloom + Kinship
SparkDamage and stuns 25% strongerStatic + Chain lightning
EchoReturns, rewinds and repeats 25% sooner or strongerRewind + Echoes
VeilIllusions and disguises last 25% longerMirror images + Borrowed Face

8.3 Dissonances

When a realm holds laws with opposite notes, they clash. A dissonance raises both laws' stability cost by 25% and adds a visible, unpredictable effect. Some players will choose dissonance on purpose, to make their islands chaotic for raiders.

ClashEffect in the realmWhat it looks like
Flow against WeightGusts and lulls: everyone's speed changes by ±20% at random every 10 secondsCharacters lurch and stall
Glow against HushFlicker: every 15 seconds the realm goes fully bright or fully dark for 3 secondsLight strobes across the island
Bloom against SparkWildfire: hedges and grass hit by any spark effect burn for 5 seconds, hurting anyone insideSmall flames race through greenery
Echo against VeilDéjà vu: once per heist, an illusion of the crew appears somewhere else and draws guardsA ghostly copy of the crew

8.5 Chords

A chord is three different notes, none of them opposites, carried by laws in the same realm (crown laws count). Chords are the late-game discovery: they need three laws in play and a Lab of level 3 to identify. A chord lowers the cost of all three laws by 10% and adds a strong effect.

Ghost tideFlow Echo HushKnocked-out characters drift back to where they entered the realm instead of being caught.

Iron bellWeight Echo GlowEvery step echoes: guards hear 2 tiles further but see 2 tiles less.
MirageFlow Veil GlowAnything moving appears one tile from where it really is.

8.6 How players discover combinations

KindHow it's foundShown whenCount
HarmonyAutomatic whenever two laws share a noteWhile weaving and scouting, from the first day8 kinds
DissonanceAutomatic whenever opposite notes meetWhile weaving, with a warning4 kinds
Signature resonanceThe Lab, or crossing it in a heist (gives a hint)Once discovered; the Codex shows how many remain in each school44
ChordThe Lab from level 3, or crossing one (gives a hint)Once discovered12
ParadoxThe Lab, from two tier III laws with opposite notesOnce discovered3
Why notes

A list of pairs has to be memorised; notes can be reasoned about. A player who knows that Hush laws hide better together can predict hundreds of combinations without looking anything up, which is how Genshin Impact's elemental reactions and Balatro's jokers stay learnable while feeling endless. The hidden signatures and chords keep the thrill of discovery on top of that.

8.7 What happens when everything applies at once

A law, a resonance and a chord can all change the same thing. The result must be identical on the phone, on the server and a year later, so the order is fixed rather than arbitrary. It is adapted from the rules engine that has been solving this problem in public for thirty years [217].

StepRule
1Kind before number. Changes to what something is — terrain becoming shadow, a guard gaining an ability — resolve before changes to how much of something there is. Within numbers, "becomes X" comes before "and then add Y"
2Older first. A law woven while designing the island applies before one triggered mid-heist
3Dependencies jump the queue. If one effect changes what another does or whom it touches, the second waits for the first. Circular cases fall back to age order
4Ties break by name. Lower rank, then alphabetical order, then the older object. Because names are unique and fixed, a tie breaks the same way everywhere, forever

Paradoxes always win. They are written as "cannot" rather than "less", and resolve last inside their layer, so no ordinary law can overturn one.

9.4 Storage, exposure and theft

One-way theft (changed in version 0.8)

By default a raider's haul is created by the game from a snapshot of the target, and the defender loses nothing at all. Defenders still earn rewards for foiling raids. Players who want real stakes opt into the Open Vault league, where the rules below apply in full and rewards are 40% higher on both sides. The reasoning is in 27.5.

  • The Vault holds most Starlight and Essence. Its sealed share (40% at level 1, rising to 71.5% at level 10) can never be stolen.
  • Storehouses in outer realms add capacity and are fully exposed, so where you place them decides what raiders pass on the way in.
  • A heist can take up to 25% of the Vault's exposed amount and 50% of each Storehouse passed, capped by the crew's carrying capacity, plus a 10% bonus created by the game and a league bonus.
  • Balance target: a successful heist against an even match brings about a fifth of a day's production, so heists supply roughly a third of an active player's resources.
  • Entry fee: 2% of the raider's Starlight, from 100 to 25,000, returned in full after a clean heist.
  • Defence rewards: a foiled heist gives the defender the entry fee plus 5% of what the crew was carrying.

9.6 What a raid pays

The number at the centre of the economy, and until now undefined. Because theft is one-way, a haul is minted rather than taken — which makes it a pure faucet, and makes its size the single dial that sets how fast the whole game inflates.

The decision that shapes everything else

The obvious approach is the one base builders use: pay the raider a percentage of what the defender is holding [223]. That cannot work here. In those games the loot leaves the defender, so the money supply is unchanged; here it is created, so tying the payout to how much people hoard would tie the inflation rate to behaviour we neither see clearly nor control. The haul is therefore driven by the raider's own level, and the target's wealth only nudges it within a narrow band.

Haul = B(L) × grade × difficulty × richness × fatigue
TermValueWhat it does
B(L), the base100 × 1.5(L−1)100 at realm level 1, about 500 at 5, about 3,800 at 10. The master inflation lever. Changing the growth rate from 1.5 to 1.65 nearly triples the faucet by level 10, so it is locked first and moved rarely
GradeClean 1.0, loud 0.7, partial 0.4, foiled 0Supersedes the older outcome multipliers in 12.9
DifficultyLevel or above 1.0 to 1.2, one below 0.8, two below 0.5, three or more below 0.25Punching up pays a little more; farming the weak pays almost nothing. The bonus is capped so it cannot be gamed
RichnessExposed wealth against the level median, clamped between 0.7 and 1.3A richer island is worth more, but a hoarder can never spike the faucet. A clean raid on a fully sealed island still pays 0.7 — nobody ever leaves with nothing [224]
Fatigue0.85 on each successive raid that daySix raids pay about 4.15 times one, so playing more is worth it and playing endlessly is not

What is exposed: everything in storehouses, plus the unsealed part of the Vault, where the sealed share runs 40% at realm level 1 and rises by 3.5 points a level to 71.5% at level 10 (9.4).

What it works out to

Realm levelBaseA clean raidAverage per attemptA full day, six raids
215015068about 284
6759759346about 1,437
103,8443,8441,753about 7,278

The average assumes defences hold 37.5% of the time — the middle of the target band in 13.2 — and that successful raids split roughly 35% clean, 40% loud, 25% partial. An attempt is worth about 46% of a clean same-level haul, which is the number the progression curve is built on: an upgrade costing 25 clean raids takes about 55 attempts, or nine days at six a day, at every level.

The caps that hold it

  • Per raid: never more than 1.3 times the base, which is what the richness clamp already implies.
  • Per day: the fatigue curve, plus a hard ceiling half again above it for players punching up.
  • Per week: five days' worth, not seven — so missing two days a week costs nothing, and grinding every day gains little.
  • There is no hard-currency sink, because nothing is sold for power. The caps are the inflation control, and the health signal is the weekly growth in what players are holding [225].
What has to be watched

As players get better, more raids come out clean, which raises the faucet without anything changing. If the clean rate climbs from 35% to 60%, payouts rise about 14% on their own. The grade split is monitored and the caps re-tuned rather than the formula rewritten.

10Buildings

Sixteen kinds of building. There are no build timers: building and upgrading are instant, and the pace comes from resources and from the Spire's level, which caps every other building. Every level of every building is listed below with its cost, what it gives, and when an engaged player typically builds it.

10.1 Placement rules

  • Buildings sit on the realm grid and block movement and sight. Most are 2 by 2 tiles; the Spire and Vault are 3 by 3.
  • No building may be taller than the Spire's level allows: a building's level can't exceed the Spire's (for five-level buildings, half the Spire's level, rounded up).
  • Producing buildings need workers: 1 slot at levels 1 to 3, 2 at levels 4 to 6, 3 at levels 7 to 10.
  • Moving a building is free and instant, like terrain.

10.2 Every level of every building

"Engaged player builds it" is the day an engaged player's first building of that kind reaches the level, from the simulation in 14. "Income hours to afford" is the cost divided by that player's hourly Starlight production at that moment, a measure of how big the purchase feels.

11.3 Traits

Every ruleborn is born with two traits. They are common (60% of rolls), uncommon (30%) or rare (10%). Traits tied to a law are three times as likely when a character is born in a realm running that law.

KindTraits
BodySwift: +10% speed. Sturdy: +15% health. Brave: +10% power when outnumbered. Hoarder: +30% carry. Greedy: +50% carry but drops 20% of it when hit. Clumsy: +15% speed, 10% chance to trigger any ward it passes.
HeistQuiet: guards notice it 25% later. Tinker: disarms wards 30% faster. Lucky: 10% chance of a bonus page. Loyal: rests 25% less after a success. Shadow: invisible after standing still 3 seconds.
Law-linkedFloaty: an extra leap under Half gravity. Swimmer: ignores Slow rivers. Grounded: unmoved by Current and Inward pull. Sure-footed: doesn't slide on Frictionless. Night-eyed: full sight in the dark. Insulated: immune to Static and Chain lightning. Sun-hardened: immune to Sunburst. Thornproof: immune to Thorns. Clear-headed: immune to Spores and Delay. Echo-touched: returns once at 50% even without Echoes. Lantern-born: safe outside lantern light.
HomeHomebody: +20% work, -10% power in heists. Sleepy: +30% work, rests 50% longer. Green thumb: +25% in Gardens. Well-digger: +25% in Star Wells. Spring-finder: +25% in Aether Springs. Watchful: +3 sight as a guard. Stubborn: +25% health as a guard. Teacher: births in its realm roll one extra trait to choose from. Steady: its building keeps producing for one hour after it leaves.

11.4 Levels

Essence to reach level n = 150 × 1.55n−2 (150 for level 2, about 5,000 for level 10)
Each level: +8% health and power, +5% carry. Abilities improve at levels 4, 7 and 10 (15% shorter cooldown and 20% stronger effect each time)
Highest level = 2 × the level of the Hearth the character lives in

11.5 Where characters come from

  1. Births at a Nursery. The kind is drawn from the schools of the laws woven in that realm (weight: the law's tier + 1) and the realm's own school (weight 2). Within a school, roles the player has fewest of are twice as likely. A birth costs 100 Essence plus 40 per character already owned.
  2. Strays found on heists. About one heist in eight finds a stray in the target universe; carrying it out adds it to the roster with three traits, one of them rare.
  3. Visitors' favours, constellation events and the season track.

Every player starts with five ruleborn: three wake in the first minute, and two strays follow the crew home after the first heist, where a free Hearth waits for them. The roster holds 3 characters for the Spire plus the places in every Hearth, around 30 at the most at launch. There is no training and no army camp: the crew for a heist is chosen from characters who are idle or can be pulled off work.

11.6 States and tiredness

StateRules
WorkingProduces in one building. Production starts 5 minutes after assignment, so constant swapping doesn't pay.
GuardingStationed at a Guardian Post. Guards defend only while on duty at the moment a heist starts.
On a heistAway for the heist's 3 minutes.
RestingAfter a heist: 45 minutes after a clean escape, 60 after a loud one, 180 if caught. Hearths shorten rest 5% per level. Waking early costs 2 Essence per level per minute left.
IdleAvailable for anything.
Why this is the core trade-off

A character on a heist isn't working or guarding. Raiding more means earning less at home and defending worse, so a larger roster is the real measure of strength, and every session starts with a small decision about who does what.

11.7 Sages, the heroes

Sages are rare, named characters who bend rules instead of fighting. A player brings one Sage on each heist, and can station another at the Heart as its guardian. Sages are earned through play and never sold. (They were called Keepers in version 0.1; the name now belongs to the player alone.)

SageUnlocksHeist powersAt home
The ArchivistStartSuspend: switch off one law in the current realm for 10 s (1 use). Reveal: show every ward in the realm (2 uses). Recall: bring a knocked-out character back at 40% (1 use).Lab experiments 20% faster. On guard: when an alarm sounds, the crew is shown to every guard for 5 s.
The TinkererKeeper level 7Invert: turn a law into its opposite for 10 s, such as Half gravity into heavy gravity (1 use). Jam: disable a ward for 12 s (2 uses). Plank: lay a 4-tile shortcut over a gap for 15 s (2 uses).Buildings cost 10% less. On guard: the first ward the crew disables rearms after 5 s.
The GardenerKeeper level 13Vine bridge: join two points up to 6 tiles apart for 20 s (1 use). Renew: heal the crew 30% over 5 s (1 use). Decoy: plant a sapling guards chase for 8 s (2 uses).Gardens make 15% more. On guard: hedges and wards in the Heart heal 50% faster.
The WandererKeeper level 20Copy: take one enemy law and carry it around the crew for the rest of the heist (1 use). Rift: open a two-way rift between two realms already visited for 20 s (1 use). Tailwind: crew moves 40% faster for 6 s (2 uses).The Observatory offers one more target. On guard: raiders can't call their skiff to one chosen outer realm for the first 60 s.

Sages level from 1 to 40 with Insight. Every fifth level improves one power (an extra use, a longer effect or a shorter cooldown). The Chronicler (Time) and the Lamplighter (Energy) follow after launch.

Visitors

Visitors arrive at the Visitor's Dock and stay 12 hours.

VisitorWhat they offer

The CollectorSwaps pages: three of one law for one of another (five for two at Dock level 3).
The StrayAsks a favour, such as crossing a Slow rivers realm twice or discovering a resonance, and joins the roster with three traits when it's done.

Paradox-born

Legendary ruleborn. While a paradox is woven, the Nursery in its realm can birth its paradox-born once. A player can own one of each.

Paradox-bornFromGift
The ReverserReversalSwaps places with any character or guard in sight (15 s).
The TwinnedTwin sunsActs twice: every ability fires two times.
The UnmadeUnmakingIgnores every law, helpful or harmful.

Anomalies

Cosmic bosses fought by a whole constellation (see 17.3): the Devourer, a drifting black hole; the Hourglass Storm, which scrambles time; and the Wildfire Bloom, where fire and growth run wild.

11.9 How laws shape ruleborn

  • What hatches: each Nursery weighs the schools around it: 3 for each law woven in its realm, 2 for the realm's own school and 1 for each crown law. A Tidehold Nursery with Slow rivers and Bloom woven hatches Time ruleborn five times in eight and Life ruleborn three times in eight.
  • Law-linked traits: 30% of births roll a trait tied to one of the realm's laws, such as Swimmer from Slow rivers or Floaty from Half gravity; a tier III law raises that to 40%.
  • Resistances: many ruleborn resist a law of their own school (a Tidewalker ignores Slow rivers, a Stormhound is immune to Static), which is why crew choice matters against a target's laws.
  • Movement: laws change how every character moves (7.4), and each body exaggerates it differently: a Featherkin floats furthest under Half gravity, while a Mossbear barely leaves the ground (21.6).
  • Strays: the surprise strays from heists (14.6) are born under one of the laws the crew crossed.

11.10 Law-shaped forms

Every ruleborn hatches in a form shaped by the laws around its Nursery, so the islands a player designs decide the creatures they collect. Eighteen kinds and eight notes make 144 forms.

Note of the formHow it looksIts small quirk
FlowStreaming fins, ribbons and swept feathers+5% speed
WeightStone plates and a stocky stance+10% carrying
GlowA warm inner light and bright markingsLights the tile around it
HushMidnight colours and soft, silent edgesNoticed 10% later
BloomLeaves, petals and mossHeals 1% a second while still
SparkCrackling tips and ember flecks+5% power
EchoFaint ghost outlines that trail a step behindReturns once at 20% after being knocked out
VeilShimmering, shifting patternsA one-second disguise after landing
  • How forms are decided: the note carried by the most laws in the Nursery's realm, crown laws included, sets the form. When notes tie, the odds are shown before hatching.
  • Collecting by design: to hatch Veil forms, weave Veil laws next to a Nursery. Forms are never sold, and there are no paid hatches.
  • The Forms album: completing all eight forms of one kind unlocks an outfit; completing one note across every kind unlocks a skiff sail.
  • Trading: constellation members can swap one ruleborn a week when both agree. No currency is involved.
  • Balance: quirks are small sidegrades, so a player's favourite form is never wrong.

11.11 The character bible

Players form real attachments to game characters, and those attachments go with enjoyment and time played; a survey of 213 players found seven distinct kinds, from admiring a character's competence to worrying about its wellbeing [124] [125]. Attachment is built from small, specific things — a look, a habit, a way of moving — so every ruleborn is specified rather than left to the artist or the balance sheet. Rules that hold across all eighteen
  • Each has one habit you can watch at home. Idle behaviour is where attachment is built, not in combat.
  • Each resists exactly one law family, so crew choice against a scouted island is a real decision (12.4).
  • No ruleborn is strictly better than another. Levels raise numbers; they never turn a Scout into a Warden.
  • Each has a sound so a player can tell who acted without looking (21.8).
  • Each takes eight forms (11.10), and the form changes the look and one small quirk, never the role.

12Heists

A heist is a three-minute run into another player's universe: get in, open the Vault, get out before the way home closes. Nothing is destroyed for good, and the challenge is reading the laws, not out-muscling them.

12.1 Why raid

RewardWhy it matters
Starlight and EssenceAbout 40% of mid-game growth
Pages of the laws you crossedThe reason to raid. Pages restore and upgrade laws, a heist is worth two to three sessions of the Library's trickle, and what you get leans toward the school you raided (7.6)
InsightLevels your Sages
RenownSets your league, your season rewards and your targets
StraysRare recruits with three traits
Constellation progressCounts toward shared goals

12.2 The heist in six steps

  1. 1Find
  2. 2Scout
  3. 3Plan
  4. 4Cross
  5. 5Vault
  6. 6Escape

Steps 1 to 3: no time limitSteps 4 to 6: on the clock, 2.5 to 4 minutes

12.3 Finding a target

  • The Observatory offers 3 universes (5 at level 5) biased so the median heist is winnable (12.15): within 150 Renown of yours, within 3 Keeper levels, and within 20% of your universe's strength (stability capacity plus the levels of your five best characters).
  • Refreshing the list costs Aether: 50, doubling with each refresh in the same hour.
  • Echo universes: when fewer than three real universes fit, the list is topped up with echoes: snapshots of real universes from the last 14 days. Robbing an echo takes nothing from its owner; its loot is created by the game. This keeps matchmaking full while the player base is small.
  • Complexity budget: suggested targets respect the limits on unfamiliar laws in 7.9.
  • New players can't be raided by other players for their first 72 hours, or until they raid a player themselves.
  • Trace: within 24 hours of being robbed, a player can target the raider once, with a free scout and no entry fee.

12.4 Scouting

Free information: name, Keeper level, number of realms, Renown and a rough loot estimate. A paid scout (20 Aether per realm, less with Observatory levels) shows each realm's laws, the number and roles of its guards, and how many wards of each type it has, but not where they are. Ward positions come from a Lantern Wisp during the heist, the Archivist's Reveal, or the Cartographer's maps. A scout stays valid for 15 minutes.

12.5 Planning

ChoiceRules
EntryAny edge tile of any outer realm (see 5.4), or a fault if the target is overloaded.
RouteA path of realms to the Heart and out again. The game proposes the shortest; the player can drag it through other realms.
Crew3 characters, 4 from Keeper level 8, 5 from level 16. Resting characters can't go.
SageOne, from Keeper level 2.
Casts1 slot, 2 from Keeper level 12. A cast brings one of your own unlocked laws into their universe: it covers a circle of 4 tiles for 10 seconds and costs 30 Aether per point of the law's base cost.
Heist clock = 150 seconds + 15 seconds × links on the shortest route from the landing realm to the Heart, up to 240 seconds. Haste makes the clock run 25% faster while the crew is in its realm.

12.6 Moment to moment

A heist should feel like a string of small, tense decisions: roughly one every 8 to 12 seconds, or 15 to 25 in a run. Each is about timing, routes or greed, never about tapping faster.

PhaseTypical timeDecisionsTension comes from
Entry0 to 20 sRead the realm's law banner; get past the first guardThe first vision cones
Crossing20 to 120 sTake or skip forks; break a pylon or not; when to use abilities and casts; whether to splitGuard awareness meters and the realm's alarm
VaultAbout 30 sWho cracks, who loads, when to stop loadingCracking is loud: every 5 seconds adds 10% awareness to guards in the Heart
EscapeLast 30 to 60 sWhere to call the skiff; whether to drop loot to run fasterThe clock turns red for its last 30 seconds
  • Camera: a fixed top-down view follows the crew. When the crew splits, it follows the group last touched while the other group's portraits show its health and danger. Crossing a link plays a one-second swoop to the next realm. Pinching zooms out to the whole realm, never the whole universe.
  • Always on screen: the clock, the realm's alarm meter, the vision cones and awareness of guards the crew can see, carried loot, and the Vault's progress.
  • Pylons: breaking one switches its law off for the rest of the heist and gives a page of it. It's often worth a detour.
  • The Vault: 1,500 health per Vault level; Breakers deal double damage to it. Once open, each Carrier loads 150 loot a second until full or until the exposed share is gone. Storehouses on the route open the same way.
  • Escape: call the skiff to any edge tile. It takes 5 seconds to reach an outer realm and 20 seconds to reach the Heart (5.4). Anyone still inside when the clock ends is caught and drops what it carries. Loot already carried out is always kept, and every law met joins the Codex whatever the outcome.

12.7 Controls

Never more than eight things to tap at once, each at least 9 mm across, which is roughly 48 points, and none in a screen corner (21.8).

ControlTapHold or drag
Crew portraits (3 to 5)Fire the character's ability at the best targetDrag onto the world to aim; drag onto a path at a fork to split the crew
Sage (1)Open a small wheel with its three powersDrag a power onto the world to aim it
Cast (1)Open a wheel with the player's one or two castsDrag to place the circle
Get out (1)Call the skiff to the nearest edge and send everyone to itHold to choose where the skiff comes

While the crew is split, a regroup button takes the place of "Get out". Controls can be mirrored for left-handed play.

12.8 Guards, stealth and fights

Fights must reward cleverness, not only bigger numbers. Guards are the defender's own ruleborn on Guardian Posts, and their role decides how they behave.

Guard's roleBehaviourBeaten by
ScoutSees 8 tiles and raises the alarm 50% faster, but is weak in a fightTall grass, Stillness, or a quick ambush
WardenTough and slow; holds chokepointsGoing around, leaping, or freezing it
BreakerHits hard but sees only a short wayStaying out of reach while a Warden holds it
CarrierFast; chases and follows loot trailsSplitting, decoys, or dropping a rope bridge behind you
MenderHeals other guardsKnocking it out first
Logic: rules that let clever beat strong
  • Sight: guards see 6 tiles (8 for Scouts) in a 120° cone. Tall grass, shade and darkness hide anyone more than 2 tiles away, and standing still halves how fast guards notice you.
  • Awareness: it fills 50% a second while a crew member is in sight (75% within 3 tiles) and drains otherwise. At 50% the guard investigates; at 100% it raises the alarm, calls every guard in the realm and closes rifts touching the realm for 30 seconds. With Whispers, the whole universe hears it.
  • Ambush: the first hit on a guard that hasn't noticed the crew stuns it for 2 seconds and deals triple damage. Two ambush hits knock out a guard of equal level.
  • Wind-ups: every guard attack shows a 0.8-second wind-up. A stun or freeze during it cancels the attack and dazes the guard for a second.
  • Level cap in fights: a level advantage counts for at most 3 levels, so a well-played crew can rob a stronger universe and a careless strong crew can still be caught.
  • Knockouts: a crew member at zero health is caught unless revived. A knocked-out guard stays down unless a law brings it back.

12.9 Outcomes

OutcomeConditionLootRenownRestEntry fee
CleanNo alarm; everyone out with lootAll carried out, plus 10% bonus100%45 minReturned
LoudAlarm raised; everyone outAll carried out, plus 10%80%60 minReturned
PartialSome caught; some loot outOnly what escaped50%60 min, 180 for caughtHalf returned
FoiledNo loot outNone−50%180 minPaid to defender
Renown for a clean heist = 20 × (1 + (defender's Renown − raider's Renown) ÷ 1,000), kept between 8 and 40. The defender gains or loses the mirror amount.

12.10 Heists against the game

  • Drifting ruins: three universes built by the game each day, for pages and Essence but no Renown. They carry the tutorial and give new players safe practice with unfamiliar laws.
  • Echo trials: weekly puzzle heists with a fixed crew and set laws, scored on style (clean, fast, untouched). They reward Insight and cosmetics.

12.11 Heists with friends

  • Friendly heists (at launch): rob a friend's island for fun. The friend loses nothing, both see the replay, and the friend earns a page for every raider their guards catch.
  • Co-op heists (version 1.1), asynchronous first: the first version is turn-based, reusing the deterministic simulation at almost no cost; a real-time version is built only if playtests show the asynchronous one is not enough (26.5). In either form, two or three friends raid one universe together, sharing one clock and splitting the loot evenly. Crews are interdependent: one player's ruleborn can break pylons but can't carry loot, another can carry but not fight, a third can cast but not climb. Cooperation and interdependence each raise enjoyment and trust on their own, and together they add up [67]. Players aged 13 to 15 use preset pings only.
  • Why: players in tight-knit groups stay the longest [34], and social ties matter most for long-term retention [20].

12.12 Choice, novelty and suspense

Version 0.4 planned ruins that quietly adjusted their difficulty. Three experiments across more than 20,000 play sessions found that difficulty itself did little for motivation, while choice of difficulty, novelty and suspense each raised it [43]. Difficulty is therefore no longer something the game does to the player behind their back.

LeverHow every heist uses it
ChoiceEvery ruin offers three openly labelled difficulties with their rewards shown, and a recommendation the player can ignore. Targets are chosen by the player from a list that spans easier and harder universes.
NoveltyEvery run contains at least one thing the player hasn't seen: an unfamiliar law, a new terrain feature, a harmony, a visiting Sage, a weather mood. The game tracks what each player has met and draws from what they haven't.
SuspenseOutcomes stay uncertain until late: the Vault's contents are only revealed when it opens, guards' patrols shift slightly each run, and the last 30 seconds put the clock and the escape in doubt.
  • What adaptation is still allowed: a safety net, never a dial. After two failures in a row the game offers an easier version, visibly and by name. It never silently makes a chosen difficulty easier or harder.
  • Heists against players are never adjusted for engagement at all (19.12).

12.13 Why it went that way

How players explain an outcome shapes what they feel and whether they try again [68], so every heist result names the moment that decided it and what could have been done instead.

  • The decisive moment: "Your Carrier was spotted crossing the open ledge at 0:48" with a three-second replay of it.
  • One thing to try: a single suggestion tied to that moment, never a list.
  • Never blame luck, and never take credit for it: if a fault or a flicker decided the run, the result says so plainly.
  • Never blame the player's spending: no result ever suggests a purchase would have changed the outcome.
  • In co-op, results are shown for the crew as a whole. No player is ever singled out as the cause of a failure.

12.14 Temporary failure, never perpetual

Failure is part of the pleasure of succeeding, but only while it stays temporary; repeated failure with no way through is what makes players leave [81]. Disengagement follows when a game repeatedly frustrates a player's sense of control or competence and they revise their expectations of it [82].

  • The three-strike rule: nobody fails the same content three times without the game visibly changing something — an easier version by name, a new route revealed, or a different target suggested.
  • Say it out loud: any assistance is disclosed. Telling players they are being helped did not harm their experience in a controlled study; equalised performance mattered more than knowing about the help [83].
  • Never take control away: stun-like effects that remove control frustrate autonomy [84], so no law freezes a crew for more than 2 seconds, and the player can always still call the skiff.
  • Struggle is designed, defeat is not: a foiled heist still returns the crew, the pages and the Codex entries. The loss is the haul, never the progress.

12.15 Why these targets are offered

Version 1.4 aimed for even matches. Six million matches from 262,000 players say that is the wrong target: churn rose when players met stronger opponents, and being matched with weaker ones reduced churn more than fair matches did [146]. A short-term win rate near 50% is what satisfies [147] — players want to win slightly more than they lose.

  • The median offered target is winnable at the player's chosen difficulty. Harder targets are always in the list, clearly marked, never forced.
  • Nothing is hidden. Targets are drawn by Renown band and the player's own choice, and the reason each was offered is printed on the card (19.12).
  • Ratings are internal. Skill and island difficulty use a Bayesian rating with an explicit uncertainty term; the raw numbers are never shown, because visible ratings invite target-shopping.
  • A new island starts wide. Its difficulty rating begins uncertain and narrows as it is attacked, so early raiders are not punished for being first.

12.16 Guards say what they are thinking

In two controlled studies of top-down stealth, contextual guard dialogue let a simple AI match a complex one for player enjoyment [148]. Telegraphing buys as much perceived intelligence as expensive behaviour, at a fraction of the cost.

  • Every guard state change is spoken: "was that the wind?", "someone's been here", "back to the post".
  • Every attack keeps its 0.8-second wind-up (12.8), so the player always has a window to act.
  • Near misses are never tuned. They raise arousal and the urge to continue but are experienced negatively, through a wanting-without-liking mechanism linked to problem gambling [149]. They will happen naturally; we do not engineer their frequency (19.12).

12.17 How guards perceive

The most important system in the game, and until now the least specified. Every number is an integer, because the simulation contains no decimals (24.7), and nothing here is random: a player who scouts an island can predict exactly what will happen. That is required anyway, since the server re-simulates the result.

What each guard can see

Vision is not one cone but three zones inside a cone, plus weak peripheral awareness — the model shipped stealth games converge on, because a single cone gives absurd long-range vision or blind close range [215].

GuardConeNearMidFarCorner of the eyeTurn
Scout45°0–2 m2–4 m4–6 m110°6°/tick
Warden40°0–1.5 m1.5–3 m3–4.5 m90°3°/tick
Breaker35°0–1.5 m1.5–2.5 m2.5–3.5 m70°8°/tick
Carrier30°0–1 m1–2 m2–3 m60°4°/tick
Mender40°0–1.5 m1.5–2.5 mnone100°4°/tick

A guard standing a level higher sees a metre further; one standing below loses its far zone entirely. Being crouched halves how fast you are noticed, running raises it by three quarters, an unlit tile halves it again, and standing still in tall grass makes you invisible until a guard walks into the tile.

Being noticed takes time

Each guard carries a suspicion value from 0 to 1000. Inside the near zone it fills in about half a second, the middle zone in about a second, the far zone in just under three. It empties more slowly than it fills — about 1.7 seconds — which is what creates the tail after a close call. A state cannot fall back for half a second once reached, so nothing flickers at the edge of a zone.

StateAtWhat the guard does
Unawareunder 200Patrols or holds its post
Suspicious200 to 599Stops, turns toward it, stays on route
Investigating600, or on hearing somethingWalks to the spot and searches nearby for ten seconds
Alerted1000Calls out, converges, raises the alarm. Never lethal — the crew is knocked out and sent home
SearchingAfter losing sightTwenty seconds of wider, faster searching
ReturningAfter giving upWalks home, still easily re-alerted

Alarm spreads by distance, not everywhere at once: guards within four metres start investigating half a second later. The realm alarm itself climbs from 0 to 6 — once every thirty seconds and once per knocked-out guard discovered — and at 5 another Warden arrives at an entrance. Rising pressure with no dice in it.

Noise travels the way a crew walks

Sound follows the walkable path rather than passing through walls, so a wall genuinely muffles direction: a guard turns toward the way around, not toward you [216].

ActionHeard withinActionHeard within
CrawlingsilentLanding from one level2 m
Crouched walk1 mLanding from three4 m
Walking2.5 mBreaking something5 m
Running4.5 mGravel and water are louder, moss is quieter (6.1)

Guards far off screen hear at half strength, so nothing is lost to something the player could not have seen [215].

13Defence

Defence is designed, not built. There are no walls to spam and no towers to level: the defender chooses laws, a map, a few wards and who stands guard.

Five layers of roughly comparable weight. No layer decides an outcome on its own, and the share beside each is the design target, not a measurement.
LayerShareHow it defends
Geometry25%Where the Vault sits, which routes exist, what can be seen from where, chutes that force a choice, bridges that drop on alarm. Free, unlimited, and the layer a thoughtful designer beats a richer player with
Guards20%Your own ruleborn on posts. Anyone guarding is someone not raiding — the single decision that links the two halves of the game. Guards who have been home a while are rested and fight better, so the choice is a trade rather than a loss [212]
Wards20%Three to seven per realm, placed where the laws make them strongest and where the geometry says a crew must pass
Laws20%The flavour and the puzzle: a Heart running Heavy ground and Haunting makes every loaded carrier slow and easy to follow. One layer among five, not the defence itself
Response15%Bells, alarms, the Spire's reach, and the guardian Sage's single power. What turns being seen into being caught

Roughly 60% of a defence's strength should come from how it was designed and 40% from what has been built, so a clever player at a lower level can still turn back a richer raider. The published design of the base builders this borrows from makes the same point: no single element stops an attack — walls funnel, traps punish the route, and the defenders held in reserve are the hidden win condition [213].

Logic: snapshots

A heist is played against a snapshot of the defender's universe taken when it starts: laws, map, wards, and whoever is on guard. Changes the defender makes during those minutes don't affect it. The defender is notified afterwards and can watch the replay.

Defending pays

  • A foiled heist gives the defender the raider's entry fee and the mirror of the Renown the raider loses.
  • If the raider cast a law during a foiled heist, the defender gets one page of it.
  • Knocked-out raiders leave behind whatever they were carrying.

Rehearsals

Defence is designed, so defenders need a way to test their design. A rehearsal sends one of three simulated crews (cautious, greedy or fast) against the universe as it stands and shows the route it took, where it was seen and what it carried out. Rehearsals are free and unlimited, give no rewards, and run on the same simulation as real heists.

Watching live (after launch)

In version 1.1, a player who is in the game when raided can watch the heist live and fire their guardian Sage's power once.

Why fairness rules exist

A defence that can't be beaten makes raiding pointless, and a heist that can't be stopped makes building pointless. The route rule (there's always a way in), the scouting rules (laws are always visible before you commit) and the loss caps keep both sides worth playing.

13.1 Making sure islands get built at all

The riskiest assumption in the whole design

Ruleborn assumes players will design islands as a defence. Every comparable game says they will not. In asymmetric games the population piles into one role — one game had to offer a 400% reward bonus to fill the less popular side [150] — and in base builders most players copy a layout rather than design one, which is what the enormous copy-a-base ecosystem exists to serve. Creative communities run at roughly 1% creating and 9% editing [73]. If this holds here, the Workshop starves, the human presence that makes heists matter disappears, and the content ecosystem collapses.

MitigationDetail
Everyone builds once, brieflyBefore the first heist against a player, a 60-second guided build: place three terrain features, one guard and one law. It is short, it is not optional, and it is the moment most players discover they enjoy it.
Seeded islandsThe target pool and the ruins are stocked with designed islands from the start, so raiders never run dry while the player base is thin.
Defenders are paid bestThe largest non-cosmetic rewards in the game go to islands other people choose to play: defence rewards, creator marks, and the fund (18.9).
Design is a two-minute act, not an afternoonTerrain and buildings are instant and free to move (6.1, 10.1), so redesigning is cheap. One-tap layouts exist for players who do not want to design; they are deliberately weaker than a designed island.
It is measured weeklyShare of active players who changed their defence in the last 7 days, and who published an island in their first week. Below 15 to 20% publishing, the loop is under-supplied and the mitigations escalate (25.4).

13.2 What a fair defence looks like

Because theft is one-way and a defender loses nothing, this game can afford a far higher rate of successful defence than a base builder where losing hurts — and it should, because that is what makes designing an island worth doing.

TargetValueWhy
Raids that succeed55 to 70%Most raids should pay, or raiding dies. A third to a half of defences holding is what gives defenders something to be proud of
Defences that hold30 to 45%Below a quarter, defenders feel helpless and stop designing. Above half, raiding feels futile
From design rather than levelAbout 60%A well-built island beats a richer one often enough to matter
Any single layerNo more than 25%If one layer decides outcomes, the other four are decoration

The health signal is the shape of the outcomes, not the average. A game where raids either sweep or fail completely, with nothing in between, is a polarised one even if the mean looks right; the developers of the largest base builder treat exactly that compression as the warning sign [213]. We watch the spread of clean runs, partial hauls and foiled raids, and treat a populated middle as the goal. Comparable games are far more attacker-sided than this — one runs at around 98% successful attacks [214] — but they are punishing games, and this one is not.

13.3 If nobody builds

13.1 records that players may simply not design islands. That is tested on paper before the tool that would implement it is written, because the answer changes what gets built (26.7). The test is deliberately honest: everyone builds one island under guidance, sees a raid run against it, and is then told they may stop. Whether they build a second, unprompted, is the whole measurement — stated willingness is close to worthless here, since across thousands of people the gap between intending and doing runs at about 46%, and a large shift in intention produces only a small shift in behaviour [218] [219].

Second island built, unpromptedWhat it meansWhat the game becomes
30% or moreCreation can carry the WorkshopAs designed: a full builder, and the creator ladder in 18.7
15 to 30%It works, but only with helpTemplates instead of a blank island, a guided build in onboarding, the raid replayed back to the builder, and recognition from the first week — symbolic awards alone raised newcomer retention by a fifth in one study of thousands of contributors [220]
Under 15%The assumption has failedThe game pivots: islands are largely generated, and the player's creative act becomes choosing, tuning and naming one. Curation rather than authorship — a far commoner behaviour than building from nothing (13.1)

The pivot is not a lesser game. It keeps every other system intact: laws still define an island, defences still hold or fall, the Workshop still publishes, and the creator ladder still rewards the islands people choose to play. What changes is where the first draft comes from.

13.4 Budgets, and how a layer's share is measured

13.2 sets targets for how much each layer should contribute. Targets without a mechanism are decoration, so here is both: what a defender may spend, and how the shares are actually measured.

What an island may hold

A realm has a stability pool that grows with its level, and each layer has a slot limit as well as a price. The limits matter more than the pool: they are what makes it impossible to pour everything into one layer, which is how the "no layer above a quarter" rule is enforced rather than merely hoped for [226].

Realm levelPoolGuardsWardsLawsPrices
1100321guard 20, ward 25, law 30
5336653guard 22, ward 28, law 34
101,5041096guard 25, ward 32, law 40

Geometry costs nothing and is unlimited, which is deliberate: it is the layer a thoughtful designer beats a richer one with. Response is earned rather than bought.

What "a layer's share" actually means

It means this, exactly: run the same thousand raids against the island with that layer switched off, and see how much the hold rate falls. Do it for every combination of the five layers — there are only thirty-two — and divide the credit the way cooperative game theory does, which is the standard method for attributing an outcome to the parts that produced it and is already used to attribute win rates in live games [227].

QuestionHow it is answered
How much does each layer contribute?All 32 combinations, 400 simulated raids each — about 12,800 runs, which a deterministic simulation does in seconds. That gives each share to within about five points [228]
Is design beating progression?Split each layer's levers into those any player can use — placement, choice, pattern — and those unlocked by level, then attribute across the two groups. The target is 60% from design (13.2)
Has a change helped?About 1,600 raids per version to detect a five-point shift in hold rate with confidence. Anything smaller is noise
What is held constant?A frozen set of attacking crews, seeds and target levels, versioned like code, so results stay comparable between builds

The targets in 13.2 therefore stop being aspirations and become a test that either passes or fails on every build.

Logic: what the model assumes
  • Producing buildings hold 12 hours of output, so one session a day collects half of what they make.
  • Heist success follows the arc in 14.5 (about 80% at first, 60% after a month), and a successful heist brings about a fifth of a day's production.
  • Players save for the next Spire level first, then buy the cheapest available upgrade; producers come before everything else.

14.5 The first 60 days

Habits typically take around two months to form (see 19), so the first 60 days are designed as one arc rather than as a tutorial followed by a grind.

PeriodWhat the player getsHeist success
Days 1 to 3Ruins that teach one law at a time; the first outer realm; the first stray; a guided first harmonyAbout 80%
Days 4 to 14First heists against players; the first defence and rehearsal; a suggested constellation; the TinkererAbout 75%
Days 15 to 30Second and third realms; tier II laws; the first anomaly; the GardenerAbout 70%
Days 31 to 60League placement; mastery tracks; the first paradox hint; the Wanderer55 to 65%

Success is tuned through matchmaking: newer players are offered targets slightly below their strength, and harder targets are always available but never forced.

14.6 Daily rhythm

  • Daily goals: the player picks 3 of 6 offered goals, such as "cross a Time realm" or "birth a ruleborn", with one free swap. Rewards are small and shown as progress toward something the player chose.
  • No reward for logging in. Surprises replace it: any heist has about a one-in-eight chance of a stray or a bonus page, with the odds shown in the Codex.
  • Weekly streak: playing on 4 days out of 7 keeps it going. One automatic saver a week covers a missed week, and a broken streak is repaired by playing two days in a row. Streak rewards are cosmetic.
  • Notifications: only for things the player can act on (storage full, a character rested, an experiment finished, a heist against you). Players choose a daily reminder time, or none, and nothing is sent at night (see 20.2).
  • Nothing decays while you're away. Returning players get extra pages on their next five heists.
