19.25 Evidence review of the endgame, and what it changed

FindingEvidenceWhat changed
Appreciation is measurably distinct from fun, but no study shows it predicts continued play, and its link to wellbeing is negligible in longitudinal data.Scale development [129]; scoping review [127]; two-wave panel of 2,561 people [130]The endgame thesis is labelled a hypothesis with a test attached (14.9, 14.10)
Poorly met needs predict more hours with less enjoyment and more tension afterwards; harmonious and obsessive players differ in harm at the same play time, and obsessive players keep going while exhausted.[2]; passion research [132] [133]; 597 long-term players [134]Passion is measured, and playtime-up-enjoyment-down becomes a kill criterion (14.10)
Practice explains a minority of skill: about 26% of variance in games, and roughly 5% when measured from logs rather than recall.Meta-analysis [141]Mastery goals are about skill expression and self-referenced progress, never accumulated hours (14.9)
Mastery-approach goals predict intrinsic motivation and lower anxiety; appearance-based performance goals correlate negatively with performance and positively with anxiety.Meta-analyses of 243 studies and of induced goals [142]Reputation is built on self-referenced mastery and peer recognition; global ranking is secondary and optional (14.9, 17.7)
Guilds average about 17 members with a median of 9 and dissolve often; commitment rather than membership predicts staying.Large-scale guild data [138]; investment model study [135]Crews of 4 to 8 inside constellations (17.7)
People are motivated to expand the self through new activities and identities, and losing an expanded self is disorienting.Self-expansion research [136]; serious-leisure framework [143]Authored work can never be destroyed by another player: heists take resources and reputation, never creations (9.4, 14.9)
High monetary incentives crowd out motivation specifically in the most motivated people, and creator earnings concentrate into a tiny elite.Experimental economics [144]; platform economic reporting [145]Confirms no creator revenue share, and shifts Workshop rewards toward recognition for the long tail (18.7)
A battle pass had minimal effect on player uptake while spending rose; player themes were grind-versus-spend, elitism and pressure.Mixed-methods study of a live game [140]Seasons without pressure: nothing expires forever, catch-up built in, no countdowns (18.8)
Veterans fade over weeks rather than stopping cleanly, and departure can be predicted well in advance.Operator analytics, method unpublished [137]The signal triggers a legacy card and a graceful off-ramp, never a win-back campaign (14.10)

19.26 The creator payment decision, against the evidence

This is the one place in the document where a decision runs against the direction of its own evidence, so it is recorded plainly rather than dressed up.

What the evidence saysWhat we decidedHow the risk is handled
Money crowds out motivation in the most motivated people [144], and expected contingent rewards lower later interest [3]Pay creators anyway, from a fixed fundNo promised rate, no live counter, paid in arrears — closer to the unexpected rewards that did not undermine interest in the same meta-analysis [3]
Creator earnings concentrate into a tiny elite [145]Pay the tail, not the eliteA per-creator cap of 2% of the fund and a minimum payment at 500 completions
Paid creation can turn a hobby into workAccept the risk, measure itOutput and meaning measured for the top 200 creators before and six months after; the fund is withdrawn if either falls (18.9)
Payments to minors create legal exposure in a 13+ gamePayment is 18+ onlyYounger creators keep the full ladder and can claim later; nothing is lost by waiting

Recorded in 27.5 as an assumption we are knowingly making against the grade of the evidence, with a stated failure condition. If it fails, the in-game ladder in 18.7 continues unchanged — which is why that ladder was built first.

19.27 The three gates before any code

19.5 sets the fun gate for the vertical slice. Three cheaper tests come before it, and each can stop the project or change its shape. None needs an engine.

GateThe testPasses if
Does a no-loss heist feel tense?A paper heist: an eight-by-eight board, face-down tiles, a guard deck, and a metronome at one beat every four seconds standing in for the clock. Eight to twelve people, two heists eachMedian tension of 3 out of 4 on the three-item tension scale [221], a median of 6 out of 10 on the single question, and at least 60% choosing to play again — the only measure here that is behaviour rather than opinion
Will anyone build a defence?The forced-then-free test in 13.3. Fifteen to twenty peopleDepends on the rate, and decides the shape of the game rather than passing or failing (13.3)
Does the simulation run on a real phone?Two weeks proving one function returns the same checksum on a desktop, on the server, on a cheap Android and on an iPhone, and that the build survives store ingestion (24.2)All four agree exactly. If not, the fallback ladder in 24.7 decides the language

Why tension does not need loss. The worry that a defender losing nothing means nothing is at stake is not supported: arousal comes from uncertainty about your own outcome under time pressure, and near-misses raise it even when nothing is lost, more so when the player chose the action [149]. A raider who gains on success and merely fails to gain on capture is a near-miss engine.

Every threshold above is a judgement call chosen for signal strength, not a number from the literature, and a sample of ten to twenty can show a large effect but not measure a small one.

20Wellbeing, safety and age

20.1 Audience and rating

  • Core audience: ages 16 to 34, with 25 to 34 at its heart. Players 35 and older are welcome. People aged 25 to 44 make up about half of all players worldwide, and interest in strategy stays stable with age while the appetite for competition falls, so planning and cooperation keep older players [25].
  • Why complexity is budgeted: across 1.57 million players surveyed since 2015, interest in long-term planning has declined [25]. The complexity budget in 7.9 answers this.
  • Rating: 13+ on the App Store, chosen on purpose even though the content alone would likely rate 9+; Apple lets developers set a higher rating to match their minimum age [25]. The matching rating is used on Google Play.
  • Age check: at first launch the game asks the platform for the player's age band (under 13, 13 to 15, 16 to 17, or 18 and over) instead of a birthdate. Players under 13 are told the game is for 13 and up, and no account is created.
  • Marketing: aimed at ages 18 to 34, with short clips of heists and law combinations. No marketing aimed at people under 18.

20.2 Protections by age band

Setting13 to 1516 and 1718 and over
ChatPreset phrases and emotes onlyPreset by default; filtered free chat only after an explicit confirmationFiltered free chat
ProfilePrivatePrivate by defaultPlayer's choice
Notifications at nightNever, 21:00 to 08:00Never, 22:00 to 08:00Off 22:00 to 08:00 by default
Play-time reminderEvery 60 minutesEvery 90 minutes by defaultOptional
PurchasesFamily approval where set up; €25 a month cap€50 a month capMonthly spending summary
Tracking and advertisingNoneNoneNone; Ruleborn has no ads

20.3 Guardrails for everyone

  • No paid randomness of any kind, and odds shown for every random reward.
  • No power, speed or skipped waiting for money.
  • Nothing decays or weakens while a player is away.
  • No obligations: missing co-op events, donations or anomalies costs nothing.
  • No grind: no reward needs weeks of repetitive play, and repeatable rewards have daily and weekly caps.
  • Losses are capped and results show what was kept.
  • Every session can end with a short summary and a one-tap "Was this worth your time?" rating.

20.4 Moderation

  • A word filter in every supported language, for chat, player names and constellation names.
  • Report and block from any name or message; reports reviewed by a person within 24 hours.
  • Repeat offenders are muted, then banned. Constellation leaders can mute members.
  • A part-time community moderator from the beta onward.

20.5 Privacy

  • Collect only what's needed to run the game; no advertising identifiers; analytics are pseudonymous.
  • Age bands instead of birthdates. The age of digital consent varies across the EU from 13 to 16 (Portugal's is 13), so consent follows the player's country.
  • Account and data deletion from inside the game.

20.6 Accessibility and languages

  • School colours always paired with shapes (7.9), and palettes tested for the common forms of colour blindness.
  • Adjustable text size, left-handed controls, reduced motion, switchable haptics, and no information carried by sound alone.
  • Languages at launch: English and Portuguese (Portugal and Brazil). Spanish, French and German next.

20.7 Creation and sharing by age band

Feature13 to 1516 and 1718 and over
Publishing Workshop islandsYes, names from word listsYesYes
Browsing Workshop islandsCurated lists onlyAllAll
Sharing clips outside the gameNoAfter a confirmationYes
Challenge linksTo in-game friends onlyYesYes
Co-op heistsFriends only, preset pingsFriends and constellationFriends and constellation
Trading rulebornWithin the constellationWithin the constellationWithin the constellation

20.8 Accessibility in full

Roughly a fifth to a third of players report a disability, depending on the survey, and platform holders now count hundreds of millions of players with disabilities [53]. Accessibility is therefore both right and a serious part of the reach a game of this ambition needs.

AreaWhat Ruleborn does
SeeingEvery school has a shape as well as a colour, and every note a symbol; palettes tested for the three common forms of colour blindness; text size adjustable to 200%; a high-contrast mode; no information carried by colour alone; law names always written out, never only as icons.
HearingNo information carried by sound alone; every alarm and cue has a visual and a haptic form; captions for the few spoken lines; separate volume for music, effects and alerts.
MovingNo action needs more than one finger; nothing needs a fast tap, a double tap or a drag that can't also be done as two taps; controls can be mirrored for left-handed play and moved; hold times adjustable; the heist can be paused at any time in ruins and rehearsals.
UnderstandingPlain language throughout (1.4); one new idea per session (15); every rule visible on screen when it matters; a slower mode for ruins that runs the simulation at 75% speed; no reading speed requirements on banners, which stay until dismissed if the player chooses.
ComfortReduced-motion mode removes swoops and most particles; no flashing above three flashes a second; screen shake can be switched off; haptics adjustable or off.
Screen readersEvery menu, card and result works with VoiceOver and TalkBack; the universe map can be read realm by realm.
TestingPlayers with disabilities are paid participants in playtests from the vertical slice onward, not only at the end.
HonestyThe store page lists exactly which accessibility features exist, so nobody buys into a barrier.

20.9 Why minors default to preset chat

No study directly compares preset-phrase chat with filtered free chat for minors — a real gap. What exists is prevalence: one in three boys aged 9 to 12 reported an online sexual interaction in 2024 [151], 40% of minors report being approached by someone they believed was trying to manipulate them [152], and recorded offences of sexual communication with a child rose 89% over six years in one country's police data [153]. The recurring pattern in every safety authority's guidance is that offenders move the conversation off-platform, which free text enables and preset phrases do not.

  • Everyone under 18 starts on preset chat. 16 and 17 year olds can move to filtered free chat after an explicit confirmation; 13 to 15 cannot.
  • Known material is caught by hash-matching, which is cheap and reliable; classifiers, which run at 70 to 97% accuracy depending on the task [154], add coverage for new material, with human review behind them.
  • Reporting is prominent, because even among harmed minors only about half use a reporting feature [152].
  • Moderation protects new players first. Analysing 2.5 million players and 18.25 million matches, toxic teammates significantly predicted newcomers quitting but had no significant effect on players past level 30 [155]. Moderation effort is spent where it changes outcomes.

20.10 The cheapest safe configuration

Three design decisions remove most of the moderation cost and nearly all of the legal exposure, and they are recorded here as decisions rather than as savings.

DecisionWhat it avoids
No player-uploaded images, ever. Workshop islands are structured data — laws, terrain, guards, layout — not filesHosting images creates a legal duty to detect and report child sexual abuse material. The detection services that exist are priced for platforms, not for one person [184]. Designing images out removes the duty and the bill together
Preset-phrase chat for everyone under 18 (20.2)Most grooming risk, most moderation volume and most consent machinery
No advertising SDKs and no cross-app trackingThe tracking prompt, most consent requirements, and the hardest parts of the privacy declarations
  • Free automated moderation runs in front of any player-written text; a paid service is only needed if free chat is ever opened, and is cheap per message even then [185].
  • Support is self-service first: an in-game help section and a ticket form. Deflection of roughly 40 to 70% is normal when self-service is done well [186].
  • Volunteers may triage reports inside their constellation; they never see personal data and never decide bans.
  • What cannot be avoided: truthful privacy declarations on both stores, a real privacy policy and terms, answering deletion requests, the age gate, and tax filing.

20.11 What the stores and the law require, all of which is free to build

ObligationWhat it means here
Apple's user-content rulesA filter on published content, a way to report it, action on a report within 24 hours including removing the content and the account behind it, a way to block another player, published contact details, and account deletion inside the app [194]
Google's user-content policyOngoing moderation, in-app reporting and blocking, a terms-of-use gate, and a truthful data-safety declaration
The European Digital Services ActA notice-and-action route, a reason given to anyone whose content is restricted, a single point of contact and clear terms. The heavier platform duties do not apply to a micro-enterprise [195]
Children's privacy lawA neutral age gate, no accounts below 13, and immediate deletion of anything collected from someone who turns out to be younger. Penalties are per-violation and large, so the gate is not decorative [196]

None of this costs money. All of it costs attention, and the 24-hour rule in particular is a commitment one person must be able to keep — which is another reason the Workshop carries no images and chat carries no free text.

20.12 Islands of players who leave

CaseWhat happens to their islands
An account is deletedPersonal details are erased or severed. The island itself — terrain, guards, laws — is not personal data once the name is gone, so it may remain as an unnamed derelict in the ruins, or be withdrawn entirely at the player's request. Erasure completes within thirty days, backups included, with a log kept
An account is bannedTheir islands leave matchmaking and the Workshop immediately. The minimum identifiers needed to enforce the ban are kept, which the law allows
Limits on publishingBetween five and ten published islands per account, with a storage quota per account. Islands are small structured data (20.10), so the quota is generous — but it is enforced at the point of upload, because it is also the cost control

21Look and feel

A guide for Claude Design and for building the world in Godot: how the islands, buildings, characters, laws and interface look, move and sound. The principle behind all of it: every rule must be visible, and everything must read at thumb size.

21.1 Direction and camera

TopicRule
StylePicture-book dioramas floating in a violet sky: chunky, soft-edged, toy-like shapes; warm light on the islands and cool shadows beneath; gentle physical humour in every animation.
ReadabilitySilhouette first. Every character, building and law signature must be recognisable as a dark shape at 32 points tall.
Home cameraAn orthographic diorama view at a 35° pitch in a tall frame, rotatable in 90° steps, with three zoom levels: the whole universe, one realm, and a close-up. The universe is arranged as a vertical column of islands rather than a wide row, so it fits a portrait screen. Islands hang over the sky with roots and waterfalls beneath.
Heist cameraA closer follow camera at 50° pitch showing about 12 tiles across; a one-second swoop between realms; pinch to see a whole realm (12.6).
ScaleOne tile is one metre. Ruleborn stand 0.5 to 1.4 metres, Sages about 1.5, buildings 2 to 6 metres. A realm is 10 to 14 tiles across, with a rim of cliffs and hanging roots.
ScreenPortrait-first, designed for 9:19.5, one-handed, with every frequently used control inside comfortable thumb reach in the lower two-thirds. Heists can be rotated to landscape for a wider view. Primary controls are at least 9 mm across — about 48 points — because real-world tap error only flattens near 9 to 10 mm and rises above 40% below 8 mm, measured across 120 million touch events [174]. Nothing interactive sits in a screen corner, where error rates are worst. Safe areas respected; nothing important within 44 points of the notch or home bar.

21.3 Rendering and performance

  • Shading: a three-step toon ramp with coloured shadows tinted toward violet, a soft rim light, and 1.5-pixel ink outlines. Hand-painted gradient textures only; no photographic textures. The toon, outline, water, waterfall and sky shaders already exist from the mock-ups.
  • Effects: law signatures use particles, vertex animation and screen-space tints, never full-screen post-processing on the phone.
  • Budgets: characters 3,000 to 6,000 triangles, buildings 2,000 to 8,000, a whole realm 25,000 to 40,000, under 150 draw calls on screen.
  • Frame rate: 60 frames a second on iPhone 12 and newer, never below 30 on the oldest supported phone.

21.6 Characters

  • Shape, to the cuteness rules: two to two and a half heads tall; the skull wider than the jaw; eyes at or below the vertical midline of the face, each at least a fifth of face width, set wide apart; small nose and mouth; short limbs; a rounded silhouette with no sharp points. These proportions reliably raise perceived cuteness and the urge to look after something, and the effect works on animals and invented creatures as much as on infants (19.19). Each ruleborn's school colour is its main colour, and its school shape appears as a marking.
  • Role accessories: Scouts wear goggles, Wardens carry a shield, Breakers a hammer or horn, Carriers a big pack, Menders a satchel of leaves. As guards, ruleborn add a sash and a small lantern.
  • Guards on screen: a soft fan of light shows each guard's vision cone, and a pip over its head fills white, then yellow, then red with awareness.
  • Animation set: two idles, walk, run, carry, climb, leap, slide, wade, ability, hit, knocked out (dizzy stars, then a puff of petals as it goes home), celebrate, nap, and one work loop per building.
  • Every creature passes the squint test: recognisable from its silhouette alone, in black, at 32 points. A form that only differs by colour has failed.
  • Forms: each of the eight forms (11.10) changes a ruleborn's pattern, glow and one accessory in its note's colour, using shared materials, so 144 forms need 18 models, not 144.
  • Laws as modifiers: law signatures are procedural changes to the shared animations (gravity, speed, lean, squash and stretch, time scale, trails), so 48 laws don't need 48 sets of animation. Each body exaggerates them differently: the lighter the body, the bigger the effect.

21.8 Interface

TopicRule
TypeBody text is at least 16 pixels, and a line carries at least 13 characters, below which reading speed falls sharply [175]. Contrast meets 4.5:1, checked against a perceptual model as well, because the standard formula overstates contrast on dark backgrounds. A rounded, friendly sans (Baloo 2) for labels and numbers, with tabular numerals; Marcellus for titles and law names. Nothing smaller than 13 points.
ColoursInk #221C3A on paper panels at 85% opacity over the world; gold for main actions, red #E2536B for alarms, green #3FBF7F for success.
Home layoutResources with storage bars at the top left; Keeper level and Renown at the top right; the stability band in the top centre; build, weave and terrain tools at the bottom left; a large skiff-shaped Heist button at the bottom right; alerts down the left edge.
Heist layoutClock and alarm meter at the top centre; loot and Vault progress at the top right; the law banner at the top left; crew portraits at the bottom left; Sage, cast and Get out at the bottom right.
IconsRounded shapes with a 2-point outline, flat colour and the school shape where relevant; drawn on a 24-point grid.
Motion150 to 250 milliseconds, easing out; buttons squash slightly when pressed; rewards fly into their counter. Screen shake never above 4 pixels. Reduced motion removes swoops and most particles.
HapticsA light tap on buttons, a medium pulse on abilities and pylon breaks, a success pattern on escape, a warning pattern on alarm.
SoundTreated as a fun variable, not decoration: sound and music raise enjoyment, flow and immersion, with a small to moderate effect on how positive players feel [71] [72]. Music, effects and alerts have separate volumes, and music can be turned off without losing information, since music a player dislikes lowers immersion [71]. Each school has an instrument: flute for Motion, glass marimba for Matter, celesta and ticking for Time, plucked electric strings for Energy, kalimba and birdsong for Life, choir and bells for Spirit. The music adds a layer for each school in the current realm, and percussion when an alarm sounds. Every law also has a sound signature, so a player can hear which rules are running with the screen half-watched, and every reveal is teased with a two-second cue before it lands (19.16).

21.10 The two tests every realm and screen must pass

  • The grayscale thumbnail test. Shrink a screenshot to thumbnail size and remove the colour: the realm should still be identifiable and the important elements still readable. Value structure first, colour second.
  • Five-second recognisability. A one-second clip of any realm should be named correctly by most players. Each realm owns a distinct value range, hue territory and soundscape (21.4).
  • Hero features against ambient ones. Of the 39 terrain features, only the handful that change a route are drawn to be individually read; the rest are texture. Search time rises roughly 28 to 45 milliseconds per item when things must be told apart [176], so most of the board must not need telling apart.

21.11 Made, not licensed

Nothing in this game is paid for. The world is generated in code — meshes, shaders, palettes, the music layers — which is both the art direction (21.1) and the licensing position: there is no third party to credit, no attribution chain to maintain and nothing that can be withdrawn.

Where something must come from outsideRule
FontsOpen Font Licence only, which explicitly permits embedding in an application and does not affect the game's own licence [197]
Sound, if any is not generatedPublic-domain dedication only. No attribution licences, no share-alike, no non-commercial clauses
CodePermissive licences only — the engine itself is one, and charges no royalty
Everything elseMade for this game
The traps this avoids

"Royalty-free" means no fee per use, not free and not without obligations. Attribution licences create a chain that must be kept accurate forever. Share-alike can reach into what you build with it. Non-commercial licences cannot be used in a game that earns anything. Many typefaces are licensed for documents and forbid embedding in software. A licence ledger records the source, the licence and the link for every outside file, and it is the only defence if any of this is ever questioned. The ledger's first entries are the two typefaces — Baloo 2 for interface text and Marcellus for titles — both under the open font licence, which permits embedding in a commercial application without affecting the game's own licence, provided the licence text ships with it. It does, in the legal page of the settings.

21.12 Showing what a guard can see

The detection model in 12.17 is only fair if it is visible. The rules that make it readable are borrowed from the stealth games that solved this on small screens [222].

  • One shape at a time. The selected guard's vision is drawn; the others show only their facing. Five overlapping cones on a phone is noise.
  • Sharp edges, no gradients. A tile is inside or outside. Soft fades hide exactly the information the player needs.
  • The fill travels. When a guard begins to notice something, the fill moves visibly from its eyes toward the crew — so the player sees how much time is left rather than reading a number.
  • Every guard shares the same shapes, scaled by archetype, so the rule is learned once rather than five times.
  • Tall grass, shade and cover are drawn as ground, not as effects, and are legible in a still screenshot.

22Monetisation

Money buys looks and a season pass. It never buys power, speed or chance.

22.1 What is and isn't sold

Sold

  • Starglass, in packs from about €1 to €50
  • The season pass premium track (cosmetic), about €6 a season
  • Cosmetic sets: realm skins, sky themes, bridge styles, outfits, Sage robes, emotes, law visuals
  • Occasional supporter packs of cosmetics

Never sold

  • Resources, pages or laws
  • Characters, traits or Sages
  • Skipping rest, experiments or weaving
  • Shields or heist retries
  • Random boxes of any kind

Every price is shown in real money before purchase, with no randomness, which keeps Ruleborn clear of loot-box rules in Europe and of App Store disclosure requirements. Players under 18 have monthly spending caps (20.2).

22.2 The business case, as assumptions to test

Monthly revenue = monthly players × share who buy × average monthly spend per buyer, minus the store's commission (Apple takes 15% from developers earning under $1 million a year and 30% above that; EU terms differ)
Illustrative scenarios, not forecasts. Every input must be measured in soft launch.
ScenarioMonthly playersShare who buySpend per buyerMonthly revenue after commission
Low20,0002%€8about €2,700
Base100,0003%€10about €25,500
High500,0004%€12about €168,000

Costs to estimate before the vertical slice: servers and backend, contract art (characters and interface), audio, community moderation, a one-off legal and privacy review, soft-launch marketing, and the Apple Developer fee.

Launch gates

Go from soft launch to global launch only if, after two rounds of tuning: at least 8% of players are still playing after 30 days, the average "worth your time" rating is at least 4 out of 5, and at least 2% of monthly players buy something.

Risk

Cosmetic-only games earn less per player than pay-to-win strategy games, so Ruleborn needs more players who stay longer. The model works when the game spreads by word of mouth, and when cosmetics are desirable because other players see them in every heist.

22.3 The scale a mega-hit would need

$2 billion a year ≈ $5.5 million a day = 18 million daily players × $0.30, or 37 million × $0.15 (illustrative; cosmetic-only games are likely nearer $0.15, to be measured)
With about a third of monthly players playing each day: 60 to 120 million monthly players

22.4 Gifting

Players can gift cosmetics to friends, with a monthly limit and parental approval rules for minors. Gifting makes spending social rather than competitive, and social reasons are among the strongest reasons players give for buying (19.9).

22.5 What the stores take, and what they handle

  • 15%, not 30%. Both stores run small-business programmes that halve commission below a million dollars a year, and a new developer qualifies automatically [187]. Every revenue figure in 22.2 assumes 15%.
  • The stores are the seller of record. They calculate, collect and remit sales tax and EU VAT on store sales, so there is no need to register for VAT across Europe to sell the game.
  • United States withholding is handled by filing the standard treaty form; Portugal has a treaty, so the default 30% withholding does not apply once it is filed.
  • The entire unavoidable bill is $99 a year to Apple and $25 once to Google [196]. No domain is required, since both stores accept a free hosted page for the privacy policy and support link. There is no trade mark fee, no licence fee, no subscription and no middleware (24.5).
  • What this means for the model: infrastructure is a rounding error against store commission at every scale in 22.2. The business risk is reach, not running costs — this game cannot be killed by its own bills.

23Screens to design

The list for Claude Design, in order of importance.

23.1 The screens as they look now

Six screens rendered from the Godot project, portrait, at phone resolution. They are mock-ups, not the built game: the world is real 3D with the shading, islands, buildings and creatures described in 21, and the interface over it is the real layout at the real size. Everything here is drawn or modelled in code, so any screen can be re-rendered after a design change.

Known gaps in these renders: no ambient occlusion, depth of field or soft global illumination, because the renderer used here has no graphics hardware behind it; trees and creatures are still primitives rather than modelled assets; and nothing is animated. All three close on a machine with a GPU.

23.2 Every screen to design

23.3 Orientation

Portrait is the default on phones; landscape is available everywhere and remembered per device.

ReasonEvidence
Portrait is the only orientation a thumb can playAbout half of people hold a phone one-handed, and roughly three quarters of all interactions are thumb-driven [103]
It matches a 5 to 9 minute session in a queue or on a trainOur own session design (14.1) and the thumb-zone limits in 21.8
The growing strategy games are portraitLast War, Whiteout Survival and Kingshot are portrait and won by widening the funnel — simpler interface, easier onboarding, less punishment — the same moves in this document [104] [105]
Marketing is verticalA 9:16 video covers 75% of the screen on YouTube and all of it fullscreen, and adding vertical assets lifted conversions by more than 35% on Shorts [106]; playable ads convert far better than video [107], and a playable is a slice of the real game, so a portrait game needs no rework
Rules that make supporting both safe
  • Same information in both. Landscape never reveals more of an island than portrait, or rotating becomes an advantage. The board is designed to a portrait-safe area; landscape shows the same tiles, larger, with the interface moved to the sides.
  • Phones default to portrait; tablets and the later PC version default to landscape. The choice is remembered per device.
  • Never rotate mid-heist. Rotation is deliberate, suggested once after the third heist.
  • Cost: about 15 to 20% more interface work, concentrated in the heist HUD. The 3D world only needs a different camera frame.

Landscape is genuinely better for seeing a route at once and for two-thumb play, and it is native on tablets, which is why it ships as a real option rather than a compatibility mode. Which one players actually choose is question 9 in the fun backlog (19.17).

23.4 Making the concept legible in five seconds

Novelty is a commercial liability unless it is anchored. Across 51,411 songs, every kind of novelty was negatively associated with popularity, at roughly 5 to 6% per unit of uniqueness [159]. Ruleborn is a genuinely novel concept that fits no clean genre tag, which is a discoverability problem before it is a design one.

RuleWhat it means
Anchor first, differentiate secondSignal the familiar — creatures you raise, islands you build, a heist you run — in the first five seconds. The laws are the novelty and they come after the hook
Show, never explainThe first screenshot is an island with a visible rule and a crew mid-heist, not a menu. No vocabulary in the first two sentences of the description
One dominant framingThe game is pitched as one thing, not four. The collection, the Workshop and the clans are discovered later, not pitched
Tested, not assumedFive-second comprehension tests on the store page, and store-listing experiments on real traffic (26.4)

24Technical logic

AreaApproach
Engine and languagesGodot 4.5 for the client shell, interface and rendering, in GDScript. The heist simulation itself is a separate Rust library with no engine types in it, compiled into the app on the phone and to WebAssembly on the server, so both run the same code (24.7). Portrait-first, landscape optional in heists. One project for iPhone and Android.
Heist simulationFixed 20 steps a second, fixed-point numbers and a seeded random generator, so the same inputs always give the same result. The same code runs on the phone, on the server, in rehearsals and in balance testing.
Heist validationThe phone sends its taps with their timing; the server replays the heist against the defender's snapshot and settles loot, Renown and pages.
Balance testingAutomated crews with scripted tactics and a search-based planner run thousands of heists against generated universes before each release. Targets: no law in more than 25% of top defences, success rates inside the bands in 14.5, and page income within 10% of 14.4.
Echo universesSnapshots of real universes kept for 14 days and offered when real targets are scarce; loot from echoes is created by the server.
ServerAuthoritative for every resource change, heists, matchmaking, constellations and purchases. A game backend such as Nakama or a small custom service.
Content as dataLaws, resonances, ruleborn, traits, buildings, eras and anomalies live in data tables on the server, so content and balance ship without an app update.
Age and safetyAge bands from the platform (Apple's Declared Age Range and Google Play's age signals) set the protections in 20.2. Chat passes through a filter service with human review for reports.
AnalyticsEvents for sessions, heists (outcome, laws crossed, crew), weaving, births and purchases, plus the "worth your time" rating and the monthly survey in 25.
Offline playBuilding, weaving and assigning work offline, confirmed on reconnection. Heists need a connection.
No AI at runtimeGuards and crews use hand-written rules, not AI services.
Economy modelA Python model of every cost, production rate and income source simulates engaged, regular and casual players day by day. It generated the tables in 10.2 and 14, and is re-run whenever a number changes.
Harmony resolverEach law's notes are data. Harmonies, dissonances and chords are worked out per realm whenever laws are woven, and stored in that realm's rule sheet.
Island WorkshopPublished islands are stored as data (terrain, laws, buildings, guards), validated by the same simulation, scanned automatically, and served through curated and rated lists.
ClipsThe deterministic replay is rendered on the phone into a 15-second vertical video; no video is stored on the server unless shared.
Instant playA small version of the game that can open a challenge link without a full install, where the platform's size limits allow.
Cross-progressionOne account across iPhone, iPad, Android and later PC, with platform sign-in.
Ruin difficultyEach ruin is built at the difficulty the player picked, from a pool weighted toward laws and terrain that player has not met recently (12.12, 15.5). No model changes a chosen difficulty.
Co-op heists (1.1)The deterministic simulation lets two or three phones share inputs with the server as referee.
Replay validationThe server re-simulates submitted heists from their seed and input log and rejects any result that does not reproduce. Validation is sampled, not universal: every high-value haul, every league-affecting result, everything disputed, and a random share of the rest. Re-simulating all of them would exceed the per-request compute budget and the cost floor for no security gain, since a cheat that is only caught sometimes is still caught [200]. The same golden replays double as the regression tests that fail the build when the simulation changes [163].
Bot detectionBehavioural anomaly detection on crew choice and input timing, added when botting is observed rather than pre-emptively. Published behavioural detectors reach 96 to 98% accuracy on real game data [164].
Input budgetUnder 25 ms from touch to picture for dragging, which is where performance starts to degrade; taps tolerate about 69 ms [165]. 60 frames a second is a floor, because 30 measurably harms performance while differences above 60 are not significant [166].
Reference deviceA mid-range 4 GB Android at 60 Hz, not a flagship. Android is 81 to 95% of every target market, and the low-end price tier is the largest segment [167]. Install size is minimised because size gates installation in exactly those markets.
Dependency mapNotes are the highest-centrality objects in the system: each touches many laws, every resonance and every chord. Changing a note propagates everywhere; changing a law does not [168]. The note count is therefore frozen at eight, and laws are the expansion axis.

24.1 The backend, and what it costs

The asynchronous, deterministic design turns out to be the cheapest architecture a multiplayer game can have, and that was luck rather than judgement. A heist is a seed and an input log of a few kilobytes, the device renders the replay itself, and the server only re-simulates to check. There are no real-time servers, no held connections, no video and no uploaded files. The costs that dominate live games are absent rather than reduced.

LayerChoiceWhy
Static deliveryImmutable, content-addressed island bundles on zero-egress object storage, cached at the edge for a yearMost of what a player downloads never changes, so the network serves it and the origin is barely touched. Bandwidth is free on this storage, which is the single largest saving in the design [190]
Dynamic tierEdge functions against a managed serverless SQL database. No virtual machine, no operating system, nothing to patchPublishing, validation, league tables and clan state are write-light. The paid plan is $5 a month and includes 25 billion row reads and 50 million row writes — several times what a million players generate [199]
Object storageReplays and snapshots at about $0.015 per gigabyte a month, first 10 GB free [177] [178]A million islands at ten kilobytes each is ten gigabytes. Storage is not a meaningful cost here [190]
PushFirebase Cloud MessagingFree and unlimited, with no per-message charge at any scale
Analytics, flags, errorsFirst-party events in our own database, a static configuration file on the edge, and a free-tier error reporting serviceNo subscriptions. A remote-config service is a file we can host ourselves
ModerationDeterministic word lists, rate limits, reports and mutes — no machine learning anywherePreset-phrase chat means free text cannot be composed, so there is nothing for a classifier to classify (20.10)
Monthly running cost in euros, from published free-tier limits and prices. Engineering estimates, not quotes.
Monthly players1,00010,000100,0001,000,000
Egress1 to 2 GB~15 GB~150 GB0.75 to 1.5 TB
Infrastructure€0€0about $5$5 to $15
Unavoidable cash$99 a year to Apple, $25 once to Google. That is the whole recurring bill (24.5)
  • The dominant cost of this game is the Apple fee, not its servers. At a million monthly players the infrastructure is about $5 to $15 a month, because the paid allowances are larger than anything this design generates.
  • What actually costs money: database writes first, then origin compute. Telemetry is batched rather than written per event, and snapshots expire after 30 to 90 days.
  • Where the free tier breaks: the daily request and row-write allowances, in the low tens of thousands of players. The answer is the $5 paid plan, whose included volumes then carry the game to a million [191] — not a machine of our own.
  • Budget: about 100 to 200 kilobytes and five writes per active player per day. That is the design constraint, not an estimate made afterwards (24.4).

24.2 Determinism is load-bearing, and must be proved first

The first thing to build

Anti-cheat, replay validation, free analytics and the whole cost model all rest on the simulation producing bit-identical results everywhere. Floating-point arithmetic differs across processors, so the simulation uses fixed-point or integer maths throughout, and the first technical task — before art, before content — is proving a heist replays identically on an ARM phone and an x86 server. If it does not, every one of those advantages disappears at once.

24.3 Analytics we get for nothing

  • Heatmaps without logging positions. Because a replay can be re-simulated, route, detection and failure heatmaps are generated server-side from a sample of stored logs. The client never sends coordinates, which removes the largest telemetry cost in most games [179].
  • Replay analysis is already paid for. The replays kept for validation are the same ones used to watch what a churned or failed player actually did.
  • First-party only. No advertising identifiers, no third-party trackers, no cross-app tracking. This keeps the privacy declarations simple and honest, and avoids the tracking prompt entirely (20.5).
  • Short retention. Raw replays and logs are kept 30 to 90 days, long enough for validation and analysis, then aggregated and discarded.

24.4 Static first: why this costs nothing

Almost nothing in Ruleborn needs a server that thinks. An island is structured data, a heist is a seed and an input log, and an opponent is a snapshot rather than a person. So the game is delivered the way a website is delivered.

TechniqueWhat it does
Immutable, content-addressed bundlesMany islands are packed into one file named by its hash and cached for a year. The edge serves it; the origin is almost never touched.
Binary and dictionary compressionStructured island data packed as binary and compressed with a trained dictionary, since every island shares the same shape. Five to ten times smaller than plain text [191].
Seeds, never replaysA heist is a few kilobytes whatever happens in it. Nothing is ever recorded as video.
Generated, not transmittedThe world's art and sound are made in code on the device (21.1), so those bytes never cross the network at all.
The platform holds the saveProgress syncs through iCloud and Google Play Games saved games, which are free to us and use the player's own storage.
Egress-free storageBundles are served from object storage that charges nothing for bandwidth, which is also what keeps the arrangement inside the provider's terms [192].

The byte budget. A session pulls about ten opponent islands at roughly ten kilobytes each, occasionally publishes its own, and sends a few heist logs: on the order of 150 kilobytes per active player per day. At a million monthly players, with a quarter of them active daily, that is about a terabyte a month — which on egress-free storage costs nothing. A million published islands is about ten gigabytes.

The dynamic tier, which is very small

Four things genuinely need code running somewhere: publishing an island, validating a submitted heist by re-simulation, the league tables, and constellation state. All are write-light. A managed serverless SQL database handles this at a million monthly players inside the $5 plan's included allowances, with automatic point-in-time recovery and nothing for us to run [193]. Validation is done in batches rather than instantly, because an asynchronous game does not need an answer in the same second.

24.5 The irreducible cost

CostAmountRecurs?
Apple developer programme$99 a yearYes — the only unavoidable recurring cost of the whole project
Google Play registration$25Once
Privacy policy and termsNothingWritten by us, hosted free
Domain nameOptionalBoth stores accept a free hosted page for policy and support
Infrastructure at a million monthly playersAbout $5 to $15 a monthYes, and it is the smaller half of the bill

The honest statement of this project's economics: the servers are not the cost. The Apple fee is. What this configuration gives up is not reliability but control: we depend on one platform, and validation and league tables update on a cadence rather than instantly. The dependency is mitigated by keeping the data model in plain SQL and the game logic in the client, so the whole backend could be rehosted in a weekend. The cadence is a deliberate choice, not a limitation.

Three things we will not buy

  • Any machine-learning service in the runtime. No moderation classifier, no recommendation model, no generated content at run time. Everything is deterministic code, which is also what makes replays reproducible (24.2).
  • Any subscription tool where a static file on the edge will do: remote config is a JSON file, feature flags are fields in it, analytics are our own rows, and error reporting is self-hosted or the platform's own free reports.
  • Any paid licence. See 21.11.

24.6 Why serverless is also the safer choice

Running no machines is not only cheaper here; it removes most of the attack surface a one-person project cannot defend.

RiskHow it is removed
Unpatched operating systemsThere is no operating system. Code runs as functions on a managed platform
Open ports and stolen keysNo remote access to anything, because there is nothing to log into
Lost dataPoint-in-time restore to any minute in the last 30 days, automatically [199]. No backup script to forget
Denial of serviceAbsorbed at the edge as part of the platform
Certificates and transportIssued and renewed by the platform; every connection encrypted by default
A forged resultEvery heist is re-simulated from its seed and input log before it counts. A client can lie about what it did, but not about what happened (24.2)
Someone else's dataNo advertising identifiers, no third-party trackers, no uploaded files and no free text — there is very little worth stealing (20.10, 24.3)

The one real exposure is vendor dependency. It is accepted deliberately, and bounded: plain SQL, no vendor-specific game logic, and an export of every table kept elsewhere. Nothing about the design is difficult to move.

24.7 The simulation core, and where it runs

One rule shapes the whole codebase: the heist simulation is written once, in a library with no engine dependencies, and both the phone and the server run that same compiled logic. Writing it twice — once in the client's language and once in the server's — would mean maintaining two implementations that must agree forever, and they would eventually not.

DecisionDetail
LanguageRust, compiled into the app as a native extension on iPhone and Android, and to WebAssembly for the server function [201]
NumbersFixed point throughout: 64-bit with 32 fractional bits for positions and speeds, 32-bit with 16 for angles and small values. No floating point appears anywhere in the simulation, because the same expression can produce different results on different processors [202]
Trigonometry and rootsInteger lookup tables with fixed-point interpolation, and integer square roots. Angles are stored as a fraction of a turn, which removes rounding around π entirely
RandomnessA 64-bit heist seed expanded through SplitMix64 into xoshiro256++, with a separate stream per subsystem. Both are pure integer operations, identical on every machine [203]
OrderingStable integer identifiers, sorted iteration, a fixed tick rate, and events resolved in a defined order. Hash-map iteration order is never relied on
FloatsAllowed only where the world is drawn, never where it is decided
Two things this settles
  • The store rules. The Rust library is linked into the signed application when it is built, so nothing is downloaded or executed at run time — which is what Apple's rules forbid [204]. A runtime WebAssembly loader on the device would break that; there is none.
  • The fallback. Rust extensions on mobile are officially still experimental [201]. If the first spike cannot get one building and loading on a real iPhone and a real Android inside about ten working sessions, the simulation moves to C# instead, which is a single-language path with its own mobile caveats. The fixed-point module and the golden replays are written to be portable, so that decision costs the spike and nothing else (24.2).

24.8 What the database holds

Small mutable rows in the database, large immutable things in storage, addressed by the hash of their contents.

TableHolds
accountsIdentifier, platform identity, league, cosmetics owned, season pass expiry
islandsOwner, the hash of the current bundle, when it changed
snapshotsBundle hash as the key, realm type, difficulty band, when published. Never edited
heistsAttacker, target bundle hash, seed, hash of the input log, resulting state hash, whether validated
clans, clan_members, leagues, workshop_itemsMembership, standings, and published islands by author
  • Publishing writes an immutable bundle to storage under its own hash. Nothing is ever updated in place, which is what makes year-long caching safe.
  • Target selection is a file, not a query. Candidate lists per difficulty band are generated periodically as static objects, so choosing a target costs a cached download rather than a database search.
  • No passwords. Platform identity is exchanged for a short-lived signed token.
  • Submissions are single-use and idempotent: each carries a server-issued nonce bound to attacker and target, and is keyed by the hash of its input log so a retry cannot pay twice.

24.9 Tests the agent cannot satisfy by cheating

This codebase will be written largely by a coding agent, and the documented failure of agent-built code is not that it breaks the tests but that it writes tests it can pass. One study of 144 autonomous cycles found a suite that stayed entirely green while the code decayed, with most modules ending up imported by nothing [205]. The defence is tests that assert behaviour rather than existence, and that a human authors first.

TestWhat it asserts
Golden replaysA committed seed and input log still produce the same final state hash, exactly
Cross-architectureThe phone build, the server build and the test build agree, checksum by checksum
Property testsRules that must always hold: resonance is symmetric, no chord divides by zero, no law produces an out-of-range value, no ordering depends on a hash
FuzzingRandom islands, crews and inputs, checked for divergence and for saturation of the fixed-point range
Content schemaA malformed law fails the build rather than a player's device

The simulation's golden fixtures and the determinism checks are written by hand before the code is, and the agent is never both their author and their only judge.

24.10 The shape of one heist, in numbers

ParameterValueWhy
Tick rate30 a second, fixedLockstep strategy games run as low as 10 and fighting games at 60. A stealth heist needs finer resolution than the first and no more than the second. A heist is 4,500 to 7,200 ticks; if a cheap phone cannot hold it, drop to 20 before sacrificing anything else
Numbers64-bit fixed point, 32 fractional bitsDecimals are not identical across processors. The simulation refuses to compile if one appears
What is recordedCommands, never stateA move or an ability with its tick, crew member and target. State is always recoverable by re-simulating
Size of a heistUnder 2 kilobytesAbout 120 bytes of header, 300 to 700 bytes of commands, and a checksum a second. This is why storage and bandwidth cost almost nothing (24.1)
ChecksumsEvery tick in memory, one a second keptThe first mismatched second narrows a divergence to thirty ticks, then a tick-by-tick comparison finds it exactly
OrderEntities by number, events by tick then source, phases always in the same sequenceInputs, then laws, then perception, then movement, then noise, then states, then the checksum. Iterating a map in whatever order it happens to be in is one of the three classic causes of divergence

24.11 When a law changes, history stays valid

Pin, do not patch. Every island and every replay records the exact set of laws it was made under, so a balance change never invalidates the past.

EventWhat happens
A law is re-tunedOld replays stay valid forever against the rules they were played under. Existing islands are re-costed at next login, and any that now exceed their stability budget enter a grace state: still defendable, not offered to new raiders, until the owner rebalances
A law is removedIts name is never reused, and its definition stays archived so old replays still run. Islands using it move to grace state and prompt a replacement
Any past heistReproducible forever from four things: the seed, the input log, the island and the rules version

24.12 What happens when the network is not there

This game will be played underground, on trains, in lifts. Offline is the normal path, not an edge case, and the rules below are architecture rather than polish.

StageWhat happens
LeaseThe server hands out a target snapshot, a seed, a single-use token and an expiry a day away. Nothing is created yet
PlayThe heist runs on the device with no connection at all. The haul is shown immediately, marked as confirming
QueueIf offline, the result waits with its input log and a key made from the player, the token and the island
ValidateThe server re-simulates, compares, and checks the token, the expiry and the caps
GrantOnly then is the haul minted, into an append-only ledger
When it goes wrongWhat the player gets
The connection drops mid-submissionNothing. The same key is retried and the server recognises it, so a haul can never be paid twice [229]
The result does not reproduceNo reward for that heist, nothing taken away from before, and a note for review. One mismatch is never a ban
The lease expiredNo reward, with one grace submission allowed
A cap was reachedWhatever is left under the cap, and a clear message saying so
A purchase completes but the confirmation does notThe item shows as pending, is re-checked on next launch, and is never taken back once confirmed [230]
  • Rewards are shown at once but minted only after validation. Showing a number and then reducing it is the worst thing this game could do to trust, so nothing is ever confirmed before it is real.
  • The server clock is the only clock. Cooldowns, daily caps, season boundaries and lease expiry are all stamped at submission, so changing the time on a phone achieves nothing.
  • Two devices cannot double-count, because currency is a ledger of minting events rather than a number that gets overwritten. Only preferences use last-write-wins.
  • Editing an island during a raid is impossible to notice, since a raid runs against a frozen snapshot and an edit simply creates a new one (24.11).

25.1 Gates for a mega-hit forecast

The targets above describe a successful game. A forecast of one of the most successful games ever is only justified if Ruleborn clears the gates below, which sit around the top 1% of games in benchmark data [35]. Missing them doesn't mean failure; it means the mega-hit forecast isn't supported yet.

StageGate
Vertical sliceAt least 7 of 10 outside testers ask to play again; average "worth your time" of 4.3 out of 5 or higher
Closed betaPlayers still playing after 1, 7 and 30 days: 50%, 25% and 10%; a third of monthly players play on a given day
SocialWithin a week, 40% of players have played with or against a friend
CreationWithin 30 days, 1.5% of players have published a Workshop island and 10% have remixed one. Online communities typically see about 1% creating, 9% editing and 90% watching [73] [74], so the old 5% target was above what any platform achieves.
SpreadEvery 10 players bring at least 3 new ones through clips, links and invites; at least half of installs are organic
Soft launchThe retention gates hold at scale; at least 3% of monthly players buy something

25.2 The first 60 seconds

Most churn happens on the first day, and players who complete a meaningful action in their first session are far more likely to still be playing a month later [54]. The first minute therefore has its own rules and its own funnel.

RuleDetail
Playing within 30 secondsNo account creation, no permission prompts, no settings and no logos that can't be skipped before the first heist.
One meaningful actionEvery first session ends with the player having robbed a vault and woven a law into their own island: something theirs, that they made.
Permissions laterNotifications are requested after the third session, and only with a reason on screen.
Guidance across the first three sessionsNot two steps and done. Tutorials paid off only in the complex game in a 45,000-player experiment, adding 29% more play time [9], and this is a complex game. The first minute is unguided play; sessions two and three each teach one idea in context, then guidance fades as the player shows competence [79].
Funnel stepTarget
Opened the app and reached the first heist95%
Finished the first heist90%
Wove their first law85%
Finished the first session85%
Came back for a second session the same day60%
Median time to the first heistUnder 45 seconds

Every step is measured separately: "85% finished the tutorial" hides which step lost the other 15%.

25.4 Operational gates and early-warning metrics

GateThresholdWhy
Crash-free sessions99.9% or better; ANR under 0.47%Below about 99.82% apps tend to fall under three stars, and half of one-star reviews mention crashes [157]. These are also the platform's own bad-behaviour thresholds [158]
Defence participation15 to 20% of new players publish an island in week one; 40% change their defence weeklyThe riskiest assumption in the design (13.1)
Concept comprehensionHalf of testers can say what the game is after five seconds on the store page; 70% can define chord, resonance and ruleborn after the tutorialNovelty carries a measured commercial penalty [159]; vocabulary density is the sharpest comprehension risk (15.6)
Churn early warningRecency of absence, plus the funnel in 25.2Absence time is the single strongest churn feature across published models, which reach 66 to 95% accuracy [160]
Experiment powerAbout 900 installs per cell to read day-1 retention to ±3 points; one readable cohort beats several unreadable ones[161]
Usability roundsThree rounds of 5 to 8 testers, not one round of fiveFive-user sets have ranged from finding 99% of problems to 55%; ten raises the worst case to 80% [162]

25.5 How we will actually find out

Everything above this line is a target. This is how the evidence to judge it is collected.

MethodHow it is runWhat it costs
Paper prototypeOne person runs the simulation by hand while a player places laws and directs a crew. Tests the two questions that decide the game before any code: does outsmarting a designed space feel good, and does designing one feel goodNothing
Remote playtestsRecorded sessions with recruited mobile players, in three rounds of five to eight rather than one round of five. Panels exist that are certified for testing with minors, which matters for a 13+ game [180]A per-session fee; an indie tier exists for small studios
Community playtestsOur own players, screen recording built into the phone, a call for think-aloudNothing, but less representative
In-game instrumentsThe eleven-item miniPXI as the default [181], with BANGS, CORGIS, the appreciation scale and the Passion Scale rotated to sampled cohorts (14.10)Nothing
BehaviourThe funnel, cohort retention and re-simulated replays (24.3)Nothing
  • Expect few answers. In-app surveys average about 13% response, and around 19% in entertainment apps [182]. Prompts come after a heist resolves, never during one, and no player is asked more than once a quarter.
  • Observation beats self-report for what happened; self-report explains why. Reported and logged play time diverge systematically [183]. When they disagree, behaviour wins on fact and the survey wins on interpretation, and the gap is recorded rather than resolved quietly.
  • Silent observation, then retrospective questions. Thinking aloud during a timed stealth run changes the run.
  • Few experiments, properly powered. A one-person team can run trustworthy tests on the store page, onboarding and notifications. Balance and economy changes are validated by staged rollout and replay analysis instead, because in asynchronous play one cohort's islands become another cohort's content and the arms contaminate each other.

26.4 Launch experiments

WhatHow it's decided

26.5 How this team estimates, and what it refuses to do

RuleEvidence
Estimate from comparable finished games, not from the bottom upThe planning fallacy is one of the most replicated findings in behavioural science; reference-class forecasting is the established corrective [169]
No AI productivity multiplier in the planIn a randomised trial, 16 experienced developers were 19% slower on 246 real tasks with AI assistance, while forecasting a 24% speedup and still believing afterwards they had been 20% faster [170]. The transferable finding is the calibration failure. AI is used for boilerplate and prototyping; review time for generated code is budgeted explicitly, and nobody merges code they cannot explain
No sustained crunchEight weeks of sixty-hour weeks produces the same output as eight weeks of forty, with more defects [171]
No hiring out of a slipAdding people to a late project makes it later; scope is the lever, not headcount
Scope discipline is the main risk controlSmall projects succeed around 90% of the time against under 10% for large ones, on data whose absolute figures are contested but whose direction is not [172]
Cadence comes from measured capacityContent is consumed faster than a small team can author it. The Workshop is the answer, and no public roadmap is promised that would require crunch to meet

26.6 The things that are not game design

A solo developer's real risk is not the build. It is the recurring cash, the legal work and the small number of tasks that must not be done alone.

TaskWhat it involvesRough cost
Name clearance, without registeringNo trade mark will be filed. Instead, all of it free: search the European and United States registers, both app stores, domains and handles before any public use; choose a distinctive coined name; claim the name in both stores early, since each reserves it first-come at no cost; and keep dated evidence of first use [198]. Registering an EU mark, which we are not doing, would cost €850 for one class [188]Nothing
The risk we are acceptingUsing a name in commerce creates unregistered rights in the market where it is actually used — enough to complain, harder to enforce. If someone registers it later they gain wider priority, though a genuine earlier user usually keeps their own market. Both stores run name disputes without requiring a registration, but respond faster to those who have one [198]Accepted knowingly
Company and taxSole trader to begin with, under the simplified regime; VAT exemption applies below the threshold; an accountant from the first store payout [189]An accountant's monthly fee
The determinism spikeProve a heist replays bit-identically on a low-end Android phone and on the server, and measure frame pacing, heat, battery, install size and text legibility in all twelve languages on that same phone (24.2)The price of a cheap handset
Competitor teardownTwenty hours inside three to five adjacent games, recording loop timing, onboarding, monetisation, live-ops cadence, creator model and the recurring complaints in their reviewsTime
Art and audioGenerated in code wherever possible; otherwise public domain or permissive only, with a licence ledger (21.11)Nothing
What not to do alone
  • Tax filing and company decisions.
  • Nothing that requires a lawyer's opinion — which is why the name is coined, the assets are generated and there is no trade mark to defend.
  • Anything involving images uploaded by players — which is why there are none (20.10).
  • Free-text chat at all, which is why there is none.
  • Writing the privacy policy and terms from nothing.
  • Running several experiments at once, which is the fastest way to fool yourself.

26.7 The order of work

Three tests come before any code, and each can stop the project or change its shape. None of them needs an engine, an artist or a line of gameplay code — only a printer, a metronome, about thirty willing people, and two cheap phones.

WhenWhatWhat it decides
First, in parallelThe paper heist (19.27)Whether the game exists at all
Determinism on desktop against the server build (24.2)Whether the simulation is honest. A failure here is decimals in the simulation, and it dooms every language equally
ThenThe spike on real phones (24.2, 24.7)Rust, C++ or C#. Blocks every line of core code
The build-willingness test (13.3)Whether players author islands or curate generated ones — the single decision that changes the most
Lock the simulation contract (24.10)Blocks the detection model and versioning
Specification lockDetection numbers (12.17)Blocks all balance work
The law schema (7, 8.7)Blocks authoring or generating content
Saves, bundles and versions (24.11)Blocks persistence and server validation shipping
Only thenGameplay and engine code (26.8)—

26.8 The build, measured in working sessions

Effort here is counted in Claude Code runs: one continuous session where the agent works until it needs a decision, hits a natural boundary or runs out of context. Hours are meaningless for this project; sessions are not.

What one run buys, and the assumptions behind it

About one vertical slice: three to six files, roughly 250 to 600 lines of code with its tests, compiling and passing. Around two to four hours of focused human work. This is deliberately smaller than what the agent could attempt, because reliable completion tops out well below maximum capability — the length of task a frontier model finishes reliably is around half an hour of human-equivalent work, even when it can attempt far longer [206]. Assume roughly two in three tasks land first time; the rest need a fix-up session. Estimates assume a maintained instructions file, a test suite the agent runs itself, and one vertical slice per session.

PhaseRunsNotes
0. Determinism and mobile spike6 to 14The gate for everything. Risky: real devices, experimental tooling, and the fallback decision (24.7)
1. Simulation core28 to 48Tick loop, crews, stealth, the law engine, resonances and chords, golden harness. Human-written spec required
2. Client shell12 to 20Project structure, localisation, portrait interface, save and settings
3. Heist prototype10 to 18First playable: render a replay, capture input, show a result
4. Island builder14 to 24Terrain, laws, bundle serialisation, testing your own defence
5. Content systems10 to 1848 laws, 144 forms, 39 terrain features as validated data. Ideal agent work
6. Backend24 to 40Schema, identity, publishing, the validator, target lists, rate limits
7. Workshop10 to 18Publish, browse, moderate, remix
8. Progression and economy14 to 22Currencies, cosmetics, purchases and receipts, the season track
9. Season and social12 to 20Leagues, crews and constellations, season rollover
10 to 13. Localisation, accessibility, compliance, telemetry20 to 38Twelve languages, the accessibility set, store declarations, event logging
14. Launch hardening12 to 24Load testing, a real-device matrix, a balance pass, a fix buffer
Total210 to 360Point estimate about 270
Safe to hand overNot safe to hand over
Content data and its schemas; interface screens; localisation; the Workshop; target-list generation; telemetry; property and fuzz testsThe determinism spike; the fixed-point module; the stealth model; the validator; purchases and receipts; anything needing a real device; store submission
  • What this number does not include: finding the fun. The roadmap costs building the stealth model and the law system, not iterating until they are enjoyable. That iteration is unbudgeted and could be large (19.17).
  • Re-baseline after the spike. These are derived estimates, not measurements. After phase 0, count the actual sessions per feature and rescale everything.
  • Scope one slice per session. If a task looks bigger than a run, split it before starting rather than halfway through.

26.9 Names, and what we checked

Every invented name in this document was checked against what already exists, on the assumption that no trade mark will be filed (26.6). Five names were changed, including the game's own. The rest are either coined or ordinary words used in their ordinary sense, which is why dozens of games share them without difficulty.

WasNowWhy
Echo KnightEchoplateA well-known fighter subclass in a published tabletop setting, and ours shared its mechanic — a copy of yourself that returns. The resemblance was the problem, not the words
Moss GiantMossbearA long-standing creature in another online game. Defensible, but cheap to avoid
MasqueradeBorrowed FaceA famous games mark in its own right. The replacement says what the law does more clearly anyway
Creator FundIsland FundA widely used programme name on a large platform

The game's own name

Lawbound became Ruleborn

No game called Lawbound was found, but "-bound" is well populated in the classes that matter — Stormbound and Bladebound are both registered for game software — and since no mark will be filed here, unregistered rights cover only the market actually used. A crowded field gives a later registrant room to press, and the stores answer faster to whoever holds a registration.

Ruleborn is coined, sits in a far emptier field, and names the creatures rather than the constraint — which is the better story anyway: the game is named after what was born from the scattered laws, not after being tied by them. The clearance still happens before any public use: both registers, both stores, domains and handles.

What everything else rests on

  • Ordinary words, used ordinarily: Starlight, Essence, Aether, Renown, Keeper, Codex, Vault, Spire, Nursery, Observatory, Constellation, Workshop, and all seven realm names. Generic or descriptive, and used as such.
  • Coined names for everything with character: the eight notes, the six schools, and the creature list — Featherkin, Skyskipper, Quarryback, Tidewalker, Hourkeeper, Stillwatch, Emberling, Sparkwright, Bloomling, Rootrunner, Lantern Wisp, Soulmender, Echoplate, Mossbear.
  • Other games named in this document — and there are many — are referred to by name for comparison, which is ordinary and lawful. No logo, artwork or text of theirs appears anywhere in it.
  • Every new name is checked before use, not after: the registers, both stores, a plain web search, and said aloud in the twelve launch languages (15.6).
