27.2 Decisions taken

QuestionDecision
Pitch and story"Your islands. Your rules. Their treasure." Laws are pages of the scattered Book of Laws; pages replace fragments
Where laws applyCrown laws for the whole universe (1 slot from Spire level 2, 2 from level 5) and realm laws for one island (the Heart has 2 slots, outer realms 1 to 3)
LandingOpen: any edge tile of any outer realm, by skiff; the Heart can't be landed on
StabilityBuilt by the Spire and Anchor Stones; seven bands from Quiet to Breaking
Laws48 in six schools: three common, three rare and two deep per school
CombinationsEight notes giving harmonies and dissonances, 44 signature resonances and 12 chords
Terrain39 features in seven families, limited by terrain points
CameraA rotatable diorama view at home; a follow camera in heists
Pacing targetAn engaged player reaches Keeper level 40 in about six months and finishes everything in about a year
PlatformsiPhone and Android together at global launch, cross-progression, twelve languages; PC in version 1.2
Under-13sNo kid-safe mode: Ruleborn stays 13+, now and later
Workshop creatorsReversed in version 1.4: a Island Fund of 10% of cosmetic and pass revenue, paid in arrears with a cap and a floor, 18+ and opt-in, on top of the in-game ladder (18.9)
ChinaNot pursued: no local publisher and no licence application
Co-op designInterdependent roles, one shared goal, and results never attributed to one player
RevealsTease then resolve, in seconds, never purchasable
How fun is judgedValidated instruments and a fun gate at every phase (19.5), never a single score
Concept additionsLaw-shaped forms, friendly heists, sharing and the Island Workshop at launch; co-op heists in version 1.1
Matchmaking against playersTransparent Renown bands; outcomes are never secretly tuned for engagement, and the refusal is written down (19.12)
DifficultyChosen by the player and labelled; novelty and suspense do the work instead of hidden tuning
AccessibilityA full specification at launch, with disabled players in playtests from the vertical slice on
Audience and ratingCore ages 16 to 34; rated 13+; protections for 13 to 17
Control in a heistLive taps, with at most eight controls on screen
TheftRaiders take a capped share of the exposed amount
Building timersNone; upgrades are instant
NamesThe player is the Keeper; heroes are Sages; traders are Visitors
Daily rewardsNo login rewards; self-chosen goals; a weekly streak with repairs
Eras and Law ClashEras at launch; Law Clash in version 1.2
Cost ceilingNear zero to a million players: static, egress-free delivery plus serverless functions and a managed database — about $5 to $15 a month at a million. $99 a year to Apple remains the only unavoidable recurring cost (24.1, 24.5)
Machine learningNone, anywhere — not in the runtime, not in moderation, not in analytics (24.5)
Trade markNot registered. Free clearance, a coined name, store names claimed early, dated evidence of first use (26.6)
LicensingNothing is paid for or licensed. Generated in code, or public domain and permissive only (21.11)
Why raids existPages are the reason. A heist is worth two to three sessions of the Library's trickle, and pages lean toward the school raided — primary, not exclusive, and never gated by the clock (7.6)
Law rarityFive ranks. Rarity sets how long a law takes to get; stability cost and conditions set how strong it is. Rare and deep laws are visible in the scout report, which is what pays for their power (7.10)
DefenceFive layers of comparable weight — geometry, guards, wards, laws, response — none above a quarter. Laws are no longer "the main defence" (13)
Fair defence55 to 70% of raids succeed; 60% of a defence's strength comes from design rather than level; the shape of outcomes matters more than the average (13.2)
Four names changedEcho Knight became Echoplate, Moss Giant became Mossbear, Masquerade became Borrowed Face, and the Creator Fund became the Island Fund (26.9)
The game's nameRuleborn is kept, but clearance is a gate before any public use: the registers, both stores, domains and handles, including "-bound" marks in the software and entertainment classes. Fallbacks are Lawkeep and Ruleborn (26.9)
FontsTwo open-licensed typefaces, embedded lawfully, with the licence text shipped in settings (21.11)
What a raid paysMinted from the raider's own level, nudged by the target's wealth within a narrow band, graded by outcome, decaying through the day, and capped daily and weekly. The base growth rate is the master inflation dial (9.6)
Defence budgetsSlot limits per layer per realm level, priced against stability. Limits, not cost, are what stop one layer dominating (13.4)
Measuring a layerSwitch it off, re-run a thousand raids, measure the fall — across all 32 combinations. The targets in 13.2 become a test that passes or fails each build (13.4)
OfflineHeists play with no connection and submit later. Rewards shown at once as confirming, minted only after validation, never taken back (24.12)
ClocksThe server clock is the only clock (24.12)
BlockingHides a person, never removes their island from the pool (17.8)
DetectionDeterministic and predictable: three vision zones, a suspicion meter that fills in half a second up close and empties slowly, six guard states, and noise that travels along paths. No dice anywhere (12.17)
If nobody buildsUnder 15% building a second island unprompted, the game pivots to generated islands the player curates. Every other system survives intact (13.3)
Before any codeThree gates: a paper heist, a build-willingness test and a spike on real phones (19.27, 26.7)
Rules versioningPin, do not patch. Islands and replays record the rules they were made under; a re-tuned law puts an over-budget island into grace rather than breaking it (24.11)
Simulation codeWritten once in Rust with no engine types, compiled into the app and to WebAssembly for the server. Fixed point throughout, no floating point in the simulation (24.7)
Validation policySampled, not universal: every high-value, league-affecting or disputed heist, plus a random share (24)
Store complianceThe simulation is linked into the signed binary at build time. No runtime code loading of any kind (24.7)
Effort unitClaude Code runs, not hours. About 270 for the whole build, re-baselined after the first spike (26.8)
BackendFully serverless: no virtual machine, no operating system, nothing to patch or log into. Zero-egress storage, edge functions, a managed database (24.1, 24.6)
DeterminismFixed-point maths, proved bit-identical across devices before anything else is built (24.2)
Workshop contentStructured data only — no player-uploaded images, ever (20.10)
AnalyticsFirst-party only, regenerated from replays; no advertising identifiers, no third-party trackers (24.3)
Matchmaking targetThe median heist is winnable, not an even match; ratings stay internal (12.15)
Defence participationA 60-second guided build before the first player heist; seeded islands; defenders paid best (13.1)
Chat by ageEveryone under 18 starts on preset chat; 16 and 17 may opt into filtered free chat (20.2, 20.9)
CurrencyEvery cosmetic priced in real money; Starglass only as a visible 1:1 wrapper (19.12)
Touch targets9 mm or more for primary controls, never in a corner (21.8)
Co-opAsynchronous first; real-time only if playtests demand it (12.11, 26.5)
EstimationReference-class forecasting, no AI multiplier, no sustained crunch (26.5)
NotesFrozen at eight; laws are the expansion axis (24)
Concept pitchAnchored differentiation: familiar in five seconds, novelty after the hook (23.4)
Screen orientationPortrait by default on phones, landscape available everywhere and remembered per device, with the same information in both (23.3)
TheftOne-way by default: raiders gain, defenders lose nothing. An opt-in Open Vault league carries real stakes (27.5)
OnboardingGuided across the first three sessions, then faded, rather than two steps and done (27.5)
Casual pacingSettled: a visible, openly labelled catch-up discount on levels the median player passed long ago (27.5)

27.3 Still open

Decisions for Francisco
  • Casual pacing: at one session a day, finishing everything takes about 1,019 days. Either keep it (nothing decays, and base builders are usually slower), or add a catch-up discount on building levels that the median player passed months ago.
  • Final names for the game, realms and currencies, and the trademark check.
  • Whether the Island Fund survives its own test (18.9): output and meaning among the top 200 creators, six months after it launches.
  • Whether the two weak variables in 19.4, performative and emotional challenge, are worth strengthening after launch or left alone.
  • Whether the interface says "universe" or a softer word such as "your sky".
  • Law Clash rules, ahead of version 1.2.
  • Which countries to use for the soft launch.
  • Whether constellations should later get a competitive mode.

Evidence quality28.1 to 28.3: how sources are judged, what was excluded, and a grade on every one of the 123
Decisions re-checked19.21: which decisions rest on weak evidence, and what would change them
Seven commissioned reviewsApplied throughout in versions 1.5 and 1.6; each review, the joined conclusions, the contradictions between them and the ranked risk register are recorded in 30
Research fun further19.15 to 19.17: company, failure, the senses and teasing, plus the eight experiments that settle what evidence can't

27.5 Assumptions contested by the evidence

Everything in this document was re-read against all 102 sources, and each major assumption was asked one question: does the evidence support it, or did we assume it? Seven assumptions changed. Three survived the challenge.

AssumptionWhat the evidence saysVerdict
Landscape orientation, chosen because strategy maps are wideMost of the highest-grossing mobile games are portrait, and portrait is what allows one-handed play in the exact contexts a 5 to 9 minute session is built for [85]. The wide map was our convenience, not the player's.Changed. Portrait-first: home, menus and the Workshop in portrait, the universe arranged as a vertical column; heists playable in portrait with landscape optional (21.1)
Two steps of guidance at most, to get players playing in 30 secondsThis contradicted our own strongest onboarding source: in a 45,000-player experiment tutorials paid off only in the complex game, where they added 29% more play time [9]. Ruleborn is the complex game. Learning in games happens through breakthroughs the player feels responsible for [86] [87], and guidance should fade as competence grows rather than stop abruptly [79].Changed. Unguided play in the first minute, then one taught idea in each of sessions two and three, then fading guidance (15, 25.2)
Raiders take real resources from real players, with capsThe strongest predictor of quitting in the need-frustration literature is repeated, uncontrollable frustration that violates what the player expected [82], and being robbed while offline is the purest form of it: external, uncontrollable, and unattributable to any decision [68]. Losses also weigh more than equivalent gains [15]. Nothing in our evidence base says taking things from people makes a game more fun; it says the opposite.Changed. One-way theft by default: the haul is created from a snapshot and defenders lose nothing. An opt-in Open Vault league keeps real stakes, with 40% higher rewards (9.4)
The complexity budget was about unfamiliar lawsThe limit that matters is how many pieces interact at once, not how many are new: working memory holds about four chunks [75] [76], and difficulty scales with element interactivity [77] [78].Changed. A hard cap of four interacting rules at any moment, at every level of play (7.9)
Failure is fine because losses are cappedTemporary failure is integral to the pleasure of success; perpetual failure is what drives withdrawal [81]. Disclosed assistance does not harm the experience [83], and removing control frustrates autonomy [84].Changed. The three-strike rule, disclosed assistance, and a 2-second ceiling on any effect that removes control (12.14)
5% of players will publish an islandParticipation in creative communities is consistently about 1% creating, 9% editing and 90% watching [73] [74]. Our target was above what any platform reaches.Changed. 1.5% publishing and 10% remixing, with a one-tap "remix this island" so the 9% have somewhere to go (18.6, 25.1)
Casual players finishing in three years is acceptableLeft open since version 0.3. Disclosed assistance does not harm experience [83], so the honest fix is available.Changed. A visible, openly labelled catch-up discount on building levels the median player passed months ago, shown as what it is (14)
No login rewardsAbout 95% of games use them [88], and they work — through loss aversion, by making absence feel like losing something [88] [15]. That is exactly the coercion that predicts disengagement and ill-being in the need-frustration work [82], and expected rewards for showing up reduce later interest [3].Kept, and now with the reason written down. Surprises and self-chosen goals instead (14.6)
Paying creatorsRuns against an A-grade experiment on crowding out [144] and an A-grade meta-analysis on expected rewards [3]. Nothing in the evidence supports itTaken knowingly. Structured to resemble the unexpected rewards that did not undermine interest, capped to favour the tail, and carrying an explicit failure condition (18.9, 19.26)
Cosmetics and a season pass onlyThe season pass has converged across the industry on 4 to 8 week seasons, 50 to 100 tiers, $5 to $15 and cosmetic-led rewards, carrying 10 to 40% of revenue in top free-to-play games [89]. Our design already matches it. Cosmetic-led games earn less per player but keep more of them [90].Kept. Price band widened to €5 to €10 (22.1)
48 laws is not too manyThe four-chunk limit applies to what interacts at once, not to how much can be collected over a year [75]. Expertise is compression: an expert sees one pattern where a novice sees six pieces [77].Kept. The collection stays at 48; the interaction cap in 7.9 is what protects new players
What this cost

The one-way theft change removes the sharpest edge of the fantasy: the idea that somewhere, right now, someone might be robbing you. The Open Vault league keeps that available for players who want it, and the vertical slice will test both. If the evidence for the edge turns out to be stronger than the evidence against it, this is the decision most likely to be reversed.

28References

28.1 How sources are judged

A design document that cites 119 sources is only as good as its worst source. This section sets out what earns a place here, what is excluded, and how much weight each surviving source carries. It is written so that anyone can check a claim in this document back to the evidence behind it and see how far to trust it.

Why grading is necessary

  • Only 36% of 100 replicated psychology studies produced a significant effect again, and replication effect sizes averaged about half the originals [120].
  • In social science experiments published in Nature and Science, 62% replicated, again at roughly half the original effect size, despite samples five times larger [121].
  • Meta-analyses are not a safe harbour either: compared against preregistered multi-laboratory replications of the same effects, meta-analytic estimates were about three times larger, and standard corrections for publication bias did not fix it [122].
  • So: published effects are treated as upper bounds, never as forecasts. Every target in 25 assumes the effect arrives smaller here.

The five questions asked of every source

QuestionWhat raises a sourceWhat lowers it
1. DesignRandomised experiment, large-scale A/B test, meta-analysis of experiments, or behaviour logged at scaleCross-sectional survey, single small lab study, correlation offered as cause
2. Size and powerThousands of players, or a meta-analysis aggregating many studiesUnder 100 participants without a preregistered plan
3. Independence and biasPeer-reviewed, preregistered, replicated, data available. The grading scheme itself follows the logic of GRADE, which downgrades evidence for risk of bias, imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness and publication bias [123]Published by a company selling the thing measured; no method stated; a single vendor's blog
4. DirectnessMeasured in games, on phones, with players, on the outcome we care aboutMeasured in a different field, on a proxy outcome, or on a population unlike our players
5. What it would changeIf the finding reversed, a decision in this document would changeCited only to decorate a decision already made

The four grades

GradeWhat it meansHow it may be usedSources
A — strongMeta-analysis of experiments, randomised experiment, or behaviour logged across thousands of playersMay carry a design decision on its own, with the effect discounted81
B — moderatePeer-reviewed but smaller, correlational, or one step removed from our contextMay support a decision alongside an A source; never carries one alone11
C — industryMarket and benchmark data, platform documentation, studio analysis. Method usually undisclosed, often published by an interested partyUsed for market shape, prices and benchmarks only. Never used to claim an effect on players27
D — excludedDid not meet the barNot citedSee 28.2

Each entry in 28.3 is tagged with its grade. Three A-grade sources in this list carry explicit warnings in their own right: loss aversion, whose size is disputed [15]; the three-needs framework, which a review of 259 studies found is often applied shallowly [51]; and the spacing and retrieval literature, which did not hold up as well in mathematics [48].

28.2 What was excluded, and why

ExcludedReason
"Dopamine hit" and habit-loop popularisationsClaims outrun the underlying work. The robust finding is about uncertainty, not about a chemical reward per action [14]
Vendor case studies with no method, denominator or control groupFails questions 1 and 3. A single studio's "we raised retention 40%" is unfalsifiable
Engagement-maximising techniques we will not useRead and recorded in 19.12, but never used to justify a design
Neuromarketing and brain-scan claims about purchasingIndirect: brain activity is not the outcome we are designing for
Generational and personality-typing claims about playersWeak measurement, poor replication, and no decision would change
Single-game postmortems presented as general lawsOne sample, no control, heavy survivorship bias. Used for hypotheses only, never as evidence
Anything paywalled that we could not read in fullWe do not cite what we have not read

C industry Counter-evidence that rarity tracks power in practice: community consensus and platform documentation for Magic and Hearthstone describe higher rarities as carrying the most powerful effects. Marvel Snap is the exception, where card rarity is explicitly cosmetic and affects collection level rather than strength.
  209. B moderate Collection-set design synthesis: sets of roughly seven to twelve items are where completion motivation is strongest, with the endowed-progress effect taking hold once about half a set is held. Practitioner synthesis of the behavioural literature already cited in 19.19.
  210. C industry Player reaction to calendar-gated directional farming: the long-running campaign against daily domain rotation in a major live game, where players argue the rotation removes the motivation to develop characters and is incompatible with modern design. Community sentiment, not measurement.
  211. D opinion The admired version of directional farming: hunting a specific target for a specific part, always available, with legible drop rates. Direction comes from the player's goal rather than a calendar.
  212. C industry Offence-and-defence unit allocation in base builders: defending troops that survive return at full strength while attacking troops do not, making the allocation a genuine trade rather than a loss; other games trade offensive or production capacity directly for defence.
  213. B moderate Supercell developer communication (March 2026) on balancing the distribution of attack outcomes rather than the average, and treating a compressed distribution with little middle ground as an unhealthy polarised meta; with documented base-design practice where walls funnel, traps punish demonstrated routes, and reserve defenders are the hidden win condition.
  214. C industry Community estimates of attacker success in a comparable base builder at roughly 98%, against a far lower defence-hold rate. Undisclosed method; used only to show how attacker-sided punishing games are, by contrast with this one.
  215. D opinion Walsh, M. (2014), "Modeling Perception and Awareness in Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell: Blacklist", GDC and Game AI Pro 2, chapter 28: nested vision shapes rather than a single cone, line of sight sampled at several points on the body, detection time scaling with distance, and off-screen guards hearing at half strength for fairness. Authoritative developer account.
  216. D opinion Miles, B., "How to Catch a Ninja" (Mark of the Ninja), Game AI Pro chapter 32: interest sources as data with small integer priorities, and sound propagated along a navigation mesh rather than through walls.
  217. D opinion Magic: The Gathering Comprehensive Rules, section 613: continuous effects applied in fixed layers, then timestamp order, then dependency, with a defined rule for simultaneous ties. The most battle-tested deterministic modifier-resolution algorithm in games.
  218. A strong Rhodes, R. E., & de Bruijn, G.-J. (2013). How big is the physical activity intention-behaviour gap? A meta-analysis using the action control framework (10 studies, N=3,899): an overall gap of 46%. British Journal of Health Psychology, 18(2), 296–309.
  219. A strong Webb, T. L., & Sheeran, P. (2006). Does changing behavioral intentions engender behavior change? A meta-analysis of experimental evidence (47 tests): a medium-to-large change in intention (d = 0.66) produced only a small-to-medium change in behaviour (d = 0.36). Psychological Bulletin, 132(2), 249–268.
  220. A strong Gallus, J. (2017). Fostering public good contributions with symbolic awards: a large-scale natural field experiment at Wikipedia (over 4,000 new editors): purely symbolic awards raised newcomer retention by 20%, with effects lasting more than a year. Management Science, 63(12). See also Restivo & van de Rijt (2012), PLOS ONE, where a single peer award raised median output 60% over ninety days.
  221. B moderate IJsselsteijn, de Kort & Poels, the Game Experience Questionnaire: a three-item tension subscale scored 0 to 4. Its psychometrics are contested — reported reliability between 0.3 and 0.74 and a factor structure that has not fully replicated — so it is used alongside behaviour and observation, never alone.
  222. D opinion Mimimi Games on Shadow Tactics and Desperados III: one vision shape shown at a time, sharp edges with no gradients, a fill that travels visibly from the guard's eyes toward the target, and identical shapes across guards so the rule is learned once.
  223. C industry Clash of Clans loot mechanics, documented by the community and corroborated by Supercell patch notes: a percentage of the defender's storages by town-hall level (20% at level 6 falling to 10% at 11), a cap rising by 50,000 a level, half of what sits in collectors with no cap, and a penalty table paying 100% against equals down to 5% four levels below. A transfer economy, which is why its percentages do not transfer to a minting one.
  224. C industry Boom Beach's vault: a fixed amount fully protected with only the excess exposed, loot locked in at first scout, and a guarantee that a raider can never come away with nothing. The closest shipped precedent to the sealed share in 9.4.
  225. D opinion Practitioner guidance on faucets and sinks: an uncapped faucet collapses currency value, and the controls are soft caps, diminishing returns and daily or weekly limits, watched through the ratio of what is created to what is removed and the growth in what players hold. Unity's economy design guide and consultancy writeups; converging practice rather than settled science.
  226. C industry Base builders pace progression through hard building-count caps unlocked per level rather than through cost alone — for example a fixed total of buildings permitted at each town-hall level.
  227. A strong Shapley value as the standard method for attributing an outcome among contributing parts, satisfying efficiency, symmetry and additivity; applied to win-rate attribution in a live game through a win-probability model. arXiv:2506.04602, with the formal treatment in arXiv:2404.01078.
  228. A strong Sample sizes for rate estimates: about 400 trials for a five-point interval and about 1,600 per arm to detect a five-point difference at conventional confidence and power; automated and simulated playtesting for balance attribution is established practice (Zook et al., FDG 2015; Foldit, AIIDE 2018).
  229. B moderate Idempotency keys as the standard exactly-once mechanism in payment and mobile APIs: derive the key from the business fields rather than a random value, store it with an atomic upsert, and return the original result on a repeat.
  230. C industry Purchase reconciliation: server-side receipt validation is the source of truth, unacknowledged purchases are automatically refunded by Google Play after three days, and a restore-purchases flow resolves the large majority of entitlement support tickets.

30The research behind this document

Six evidence reviews were commissioned while this document was written, drawing on roughly 200 sources between them. Their conclusions are applied throughout the sections above; this part records what each one found, how strong that evidence is, where the reviews contradict each other, and what none of them can settle. It is the audit trail for every decision in 27.

30.1 How to read this

Each review answered a different question, and each is summarised below with its evidence, its grade, and what it changed in the design. 30.8 joins their conclusions, 30.9 records where they disagree, 30.10 is the measurement plan that falls out of all six, and 30.11 states what none of them can settle.

The six reviews

ReviewQuestion it answeredWhere the evidence is strongWhere it is weak
1. Fulfilment and the endgameWhat makes players feel fulfilled over months and years, rather than merely engaged?Self-determination theory, passion, deliberate practice, guild social capital, creator crowding-outWhether meaningfulness predicts continued play at all
2. Ten operational gapsStealth, matchmaking, economy, soft launch, pricing, safety, localisation, accessibility, devices, creator lawMatchmaking and churn, virtual-economy inflation, pricing regulation, child-safety prevalenceLocalisation return, device figures, moderation efficacy
3. Human factorsIs the game physically legible and playable on a phone?Touch targets, latency, reading psychophysics, visual search, working memoryColour psychology, animation timing, stealth-geometry thresholds
4. Operations and productionWill it ship, and can a small team run it?Churn prediction, bot detection, crash benchmarks, project failure rates, AI-assisted productivityLive-ops cadence, support benchmarks, toxicity-retention causality
5. Creative contentAre the laws, creatures, realms and concept the right size and shape?Working-memory limits, endowed progress, anthropomorphism, sound symbolism, novelty penaltyMost of it is design craft, not science — stated as such
6. Load-bearing premisesAre the assumptions the whole concept rests on actually true?Playing an absent human, non-violence, moral disengagement, asymmetric role preferenceDelegated agency measurement, one-way theft (no direct study exists)

How sources are graded

The same scheme runs through all six reviews, and matches the grading applied to every source in 28.1.

GradeWhat it isHow it may be used
A — strongMeta-analysis of experiments, randomised experiment, or behaviour logged across thousands of playersMay carry a decision on its own, with the effect discounted
B — moderatePeer-reviewed but smaller, correlational, or one step removed from our contextSupports a decision alongside an A source; never carries one alone
C — industryMarket and benchmark data, platform documentation, studio analysis; method usually undisclosedMarket shape, prices and benchmarks only. Never used to claim an effect on players
D — opinionDesigner and practitioner writing, however well arguedHypotheses and design patterns only
The discount rule, applied throughout

Published effects are treated as upper bounds. Psychology replicates at about 36% and social science at 62%, both at roughly half the original effect size, and meta-analytic estimates have run about three times larger than preregistered multi-laboratory replications of the same effects. Every target derived from this research assumes the effect arrives smaller here.

30.2 Review 1 — Fulfilment and the endgame

What makes people feel fulfilled over months and years, and what destroys that feeling in the late game.

The findings that mattered

FindingEvidenceGrade
Appreciation — being moved, finding something meaningful — is measurably distinct from fun, on a validated three-item scaleOliver & Bartsch 2010, pilot 141 and study 268; cross-culturally validated on US (262) and German (274) samplesA
But no study shows appreciation predicts continued play. A two-wave panel of 2,561 people found eudaimonic preference predicted later meaning in life only negligibly, and sometimes in reverseFrontiers in Communication 2022; the main survey of eudaimonic game motives says outright it could not test predictive value for actual game useA
Poorly met needs predict more hours with less enjoyment and more tension afterwards; well-met needs predict enjoyment and energy but not hoursPrzybylski, Rigby & Ryan and colleaguesA
Need frustration is a separate construct from low satisfaction and is what drives people outBallou & Deterding 2023, grounded theoryA
Harmonious and obsessive players differ in harm at the same number of hours; obsessive players keep playing while exhaustedVallerand's dualistic model; Lafrenière et al. 2009 (222 players); a 2025 study of 597 long-term playersA/B
Deliberate practice explains about 26% of skill variance in games, and roughly 5% when measured from logs rather than recallMacnamara, Hambrick & Oswald 2014 meta-analysisA
Mastery-approach goals predict intrinsic motivation and lower anxiety; appearance-based performance goals correlate negatively with performanceHulleman et al. 2010, 243 studiesA
Guilds average about 17 members with a median of 9 and dissolve often; commitment, not membership, predicts stayingDucheneaut et al. 2006; investment-model study, 165 playersA/B
High monetary incentives crowd out motivation specifically among the already highly motivatedExperimental economics, 2022; Deci, Koestner & Ryan 1999, 128 experimentsA
Creator earnings concentrate brutally: a median creator receiving about $1,575 a year while the top ten average $33.9 millionPlatform economic reportingC

What it changed in the game

  • The endgame thesis — a place, a reputation, a body of work — is labelled a hypothesis with a test attached, not a mechanism we rely on.
  • Kill criteria: playtime up with enjoyment down is the obsessive-passion signature, not success. Any mechanic that raises need frustration without raising meaning is removed whatever it earns.
  • Crews of 4 to 8 inside constellations, because being one of 30 is not belonging.
  • Seasons without pressure: nothing expires forever, catch-up built in, no countdowns.
  • Mastery is self-referenced; global ranking is secondary and optional.
  • Fading players get a legacy card, not a win-back campaign.
  • Creator payment, when it was later added, was structured to resemble the unexpected rewards that did not undermine interest.

30.3 Review 2 — Ten operational gaps

Stealth, matchmaking, economy, soft launch, pricing, safety, localisation, accessibility, devices and creator law.

The findings that mattered

AreaFindingGrade
StealthContextual guard dialogue let a simple AI match a complex one in player enjoyment. Telegraphing buys as much perceived intelligence as expensive AI.A
Near missesNear misses raise arousal and motivation to continue but are rated negatively in valence — a wanting-not-liking mechanism associated with problem gambling. Engineering their frequency is an ethical hazard.A
Time pressureUnder time pressure people lower their decision boundary and switch to heuristics: faster and less accurate. Hard timers on a touchscreen systematically degrade decision quality.A
MatchmakingIn about 6 million matches from 262,000 players, churn rose when players met stronger opponents, and being matched with weaker opponents reduced churn more than fair matches did. A short-term win rate near 50% is roughly optimal for satisfaction — players want to win slightly more than they lose.A
EconomyA quasi-experimental study of a transaction tax plus item sink showed sinks measurably stabilise prices. Diablo III is the canonical failure: gold faucets everywhere, trivial sinks, hyperinflation.A/B
Soft launchReading day-1 retention near 30% to within ±3 points needs about 900 installs per cell. Cheap-market data does not predict tier-one monetisation.B/C
PricingAn incentivised randomised trial with 753 participants found willingness to pay is significantly higher in virtual currency than in real money even at a 1:1 rate — money illusion. EU guidance now targets exactly this.A
Child safetyOne in three boys aged 9 to 12 reported an online sexual interaction in 2024; 40% of minors report being approached by someone they believed was trying to manipulate them. Classifiers reach 70 to 97% accuracy; hash-matching is the reliable baseline for known material.A/B
DevicesAndroid dominates every target market (India ~95%, Indonesia ~87 to 90%, Brazil ~81 to 84%). Google Play's bad-behaviour thresholds are a crash rate of 1.09% and an ANR rate of 0.47%.B/C
Creator lawFortnite pays creators 18+ only with a $100 minimum and a tax interview; Roblox pays 13+ with identity verification. EU DAC7 has no minimum threshold for personal services.A (documentation)

What it changed, and the three things it said were wrong

Called wrong
  • Virtual-currency obfuscation. Do not price cosmetics in a soft currency at a non-obvious rate. The randomised trial shows it inflates spending through money illusion, and it is now a regulatory target.
  • Targeting strict 50/50 matchmaking. The large-sample evidence says the median heist should be winnable, not perfectly fair.
  • Free chat for minors. Given the prevalence data, the minor cohort should default to preset-phrase chat.

It also produced the warning that a "defenders lose nothing" rule, if it mints resources rather than transferring them, is an uncontrolled inflation faucet — which is why the design now draws hauls from a snapshot with sink-limited buffers.

30.4 Review 3 — Human factors and perception

Whether the game is physically legible and playable on a phone. This is the review with the largest samples of all six.

The numbers the evidence supports

QuestionWhat the evidence saysSource and sizeGrade
How big must a touch target be?Error rates only flatten near 9 to 10 mm. Below 8 mm error rises above 40%. Edges and corners are markedly worse. The finger's contact patch sets a precision floor that slowing down cannot overcome.120,626,225 touch events from 91,731 installations; Parhi et al. 2006; FFitts 2013A
How fast must it respond?Dragging latency is noticed at about 11 ms and degrades performance above 25 ms; discrete taps tolerate about 69 ms. Frame rate: 30 Hz measurably hurts performance; above 60 Hz the differences are not significant.Deber et al. CHI 2015; Jota et al. 2013; refresh-rate study F(4,100)=13.776, p<.001A
How small can text be?Reading speed is constant while x-height is between 0.2° and 2.0° of visual angle and collapses below that. A line needs at least 13 characters to reach 80% of maximum reading speed. WCAG's 4.5:1 derives from 3:1 × 1.5 for 20/40 acuity — and its exact factor is contested, particularly for dark themes.Legge's 20-article series; PNAS 2020A
How many symbols can be searched?Pop-out search is near flat; conjunction search runs about 28 to 45 ms per item, with target-absent slopes roughly twice as steep. Icon characteristics explain up to 69% of variance in identification.Treisman & Gelade 1980; Wolfe 1998 (one million trials); Isherwood et al. 2007A
How many rules can interact at once?People reason about at most one quaternary relation — four interacting variables. Accuracy interpreting interactions is high at two and three way and falls sharply at four.Halford, Wilson & Phillips 1998; Halford et al. 2005A
How do people perceive progress?Magnitude perception is logarithmic, cross-culturally. A goal that starts partly filled is finished faster: about 34% versus 19% completion for identical effort.Dehaene et al. 2008 (Mundurucú); Nunes & Drèze 2006; Kivetz et al. 2006 (948 members)A
How close must sound and picture be?The audio-visual simultaneity window is about 185 ms wide, so offsets under ±100 ms feel synchronous.Van der Burg, Cass & Alais 2014A
Does art style matter?The uncanny valley is real but condition-dependent (Hedges g ≈ 1.01 across 247 effects). Stylised creatures avoid it entirely. Colour-emotion claims are the weakest area in the review.Diel, Weigelt & MacDorman 2022A / weak for colour

What it said the design got wrong

  • A 44-point touch minimum is below the evidence. Primary heist controls should be 9 to 10 mm, and kept off screen corners.
  • The complexity budget was measuring the wrong thing. The limit is not how many laws are unfamiliar but how many interact at once: never more than four, at any level of play.
  • No pre-launch usage cap can be promised. Imbalance surfaces only at expert level and at scale, with millions of matches.

It also confirmed, with numbers to cite, what the document had asserted: 60 frames per second as a floor, 16-pixel body text, at most eight controls, and 200 to 300 millisecond transitions.

30.5 Review 4 — Operations and production

Whether it ships, and whether a small team can run it. The review that produced the most uncomfortable findings.

The findings that mattered

AreaFindingGrade
TelemetryChurn is predictable from behaviour at 66 to 95% accuracy depending on window. The single most important feature across studies is simply current absence time — a signal any team can compute.A
Anti-cheatBehavioural bot detection reaches 96 to 98% accuracy on real game data. Cheating spreads socially: players adopt it after observing or being victimised by it.A
NetcodeReal mobile networks run 50 to 150 ms round trip with heavy jitter, and 5G is frequently slower than 4G in practice. But strategy and cooperative play tolerate latency far better than shooters — some games are unaffected up to a second.A/B
NotificationsContextual notifications open at 14.4% versus 4.19% for generic. But one weekly push causes about 10% of users to disable notifications and three to six causes about 40%. Around 30% of consumers delete an app over excessive notifications.B/C
QAMedian crash-free sessions run about 99.9%; apps below roughly 99.82% tend to score under three stars, and half of one-star reviews mention crashes. The 1:10:100 cost-of-late-fixes curve is folklore — the revised figure for small agile projects is about 5:1.B
Playtesting"Five users find 85% of problems" holds mathematically but fails in practice: some five-user sets found 99%, others 55%. Ten raises the worst case to 80%, twenty to 95%. Usability testing does not tell you whether a game is fun.A
Production riskOnly about 31% of software projects fully succeed — but small projects succeed around 90% of the time against under 10% for large ones. Eight weeks of 60-hour weeks produces the same output as eight weeks of 40-hour weeks, with more defects.C (contested) / A
AI-assisted developmentA randomised trial of 16 experienced developers on 246 real tasks found they were 19% slower with AI tools while believing they were 20% faster. The durable finding is the calibration failure, not the specific number.A
ToxicityAnalysing 2.5 million players and 18.25 million matches: toxic teammates significantly predicted newcomers quitting, but had no significant effect once players passed level 30. The strongest positive predictor for experienced players was the number of friends in the match.A

What it said the design got wrong

Called wrong
  • Any schedule built on optimistic estimates or assumed AI speedups. The highest-confidence wrong call in all six reviews.
  • Real-time co-op as scoped. It imposes the full netcode cost profile on a tiny team for a mode that is not the core loop. Build it asynchronous first.
  • Under-budgeting live-ops content against consumption.
  • Treating notifications as a growth lever by default.

30.6 Review 5 — Creative content

Whether the laws, creatures, realms and the concept itself are the right size and shape. Mostly design craft, and labelled as such.

The verdict on every count in the game

CountVerdictWhy
6 schoolsRight-sizedBetween Magic's five colours and Genshin's seven elements; below the eighteen-type threshold where Pokémon's chart became a memorisation burden and a balance liability
8 notesAt the ceiling — test 6 or 7Above the four-chunk reasoning limit; acceptable only because notes are modifiers learned in context, not standalone factions
48 lawsAcceptable, and the right growth axisLow dependency centrality: laws can be added or cut with contained blast radius. Audit for laws that do not interact
44 resonances + 12 chordsToo large to teach, right size to discoverNo player will memorise 56 interactions. They must be surfaced reactively, never as a table
144 creature formsWithin precedent, at risk of dilutionPokémon's first generation was 151. But eight note-forms risk reading as recolours; they must differ by more than palette
7 realmsRight-sizedMatches Genshin's seven nations. The challenge is instant readability, not count
39 terrain featuresToo many to be individually legibleFine as ambient texture; separate a handful of gameplay-relevant features from the rest

The findings behind those verdicts

  • The colour pie's real lesson: its purpose is to make factions feel and play differently, not to balance them. Identity first.
  • Lenticular design: a law should read as simple to a newcomer and reveal depth to an expert. This is now the law-writing rule.
  • Notes are the highest-centrality nodes in the whole system — each touches multiple laws, every resonance and every chord. Changing a note propagates everywhere; changing a law does not. So the note count should be frozen and laws used for expansion.
  • Players largely do not read lore. Destiny removed its 834 Grimoire cards because they lived outside the game; Bethesda has no telemetry on book-reading at all and designs its 800-odd books as atmosphere. Build evocative implication, not text.
  • Sound symbolism is real and cross-cultural (976 participants, 25 languages), so note names can be chosen to sound like what they do — several already do.
  • Novelty carries a measured commercial penalty. Across 51,411 songs, every type of novelty was negatively associated with popularity, around 5 to 6% per unit. The answer is anchored differentiation: signal a familiar genre in five seconds, keep the novelty for after the hook.

The review's sharpest warning: the invented-vocabulary stack — laws, notes, schools, chords, resonances, ruleborn, realms — is learnable because the words are repurposed English rather than invented, but only if introduced one at a time. A glossary dump on the store page or in the tutorial turns it into a barrier.

30.7 Review 6 — The load-bearing premises

The eight assumptions the whole concept rests on, each checked for the first time.

PremiseVerdictConfidenceKey evidence
1. Playing against an absent human feels different from playing an AISupportedHighA meta-analysis of 25 effect sizes found a medium-to-large penalty for computer opponents (g = 0.631), with arousal effects near g = 1.2. Eleven of twenty studies held behaviour identical and changed only the label — so much of it is a pure belief effect
2. People enjoy designing a space for a stranger to fail inSupportedModerate-highMario Maker's troll levels and "first clear" culture; a community that spent years clearing 41,113 uncleared courses before the servers closed. Designing-to-defeat is a real, distinct creative pleasure
3. Delegated control still feels like agencyConditionally supportedModerateAgency survives delegation when outcomes are predictable from inputs. The failure mode is "my units are stupid" and the tipping point where a game feels watched rather than played. Intentional binding as a measure has contested replication — measure felt control directly
4. A non-violent game can carry tension and an audienceSupportedHigh commercially, moderate on tensionCozy games grew from 0.4% to 3.1% of titles grossing over $100k between 2022 and 2025. Controlling for competition, violence adds nothing to enjoyment: violent and non-violent versions did not differ in rated enjoyment or excitement
5. Players will enjoy being a thief without guiltConditionally supportedModerateTransgressive play is enjoyable when the game supplies consequence-minimisation. One-way theft removes the victim entirely — textbook mitigation. The residual tension is that premise 1 wants the defender to feel human
6. Authoring rules is a satisfying fantasySupported, but nicheModerate-highBaba Is You is the existence proof; god games peaked commercially around 2000 and have not returned. Rule-authorship is loved by a dedicated minority and is not by itself a mass-market hook — it must be tactile and instantly legible
7. Players will build defences, not just raidLargely contradictedModerate-highEvery comparable game shows the building half is neglected. Dead by Daylight needed a 400% reward bonus to fill the less-popular role. The vast copy-a-base ecosystem around Clash is itself evidence most players clone rather than design
8. The four-genre combination coheresUnsupported to riskyModerateHybrid-casual grew strongly, but "hybrid" there means a simple core with meta-depth, not four genres at once. Genre clarity predicts discoverability and revenue; a game that fits no tag is hard to position
The single riskiest assumption in the whole concept

That a meaningful share of players will design islands and their laws as a defence. Being wrong here does not weaken one system — it starves the Workshop, removes the human presence that premise 1 depends on, and collapses the content ecosystem. Every comparable asymmetric and base-defence game points the same way.

The mitigations, in order: make a short guided defence build mandatory before anyone can raid; seed the Workshop heavily so raiders never run dry; and route the best rewards to whoever designs islands other people play. Benchmark: if fewer than 15 to 20% of active players publish an island in their first week, the loop is under-supplied.

30.8 The joined conclusions

All six reviews, resolved into four lists: what to change, what to lock, what to test, and what could kill the project.

Decisions the evidence says are wrong

DecisionWhy it is wrongWhat to do insteadFrom
Schedules built on optimistic estimates or assumed AI speedupsThe planning fallacy plus a randomised trial showing developers were 19% slower with AI while feeling 20% fasterReference-class forecasting; no AI multiplier in the plan; explicit review time for generated codeR4
Assuming players will design defencesEvery comparable game shows the building half is neglectedMandatory lightweight defence build, heavy seeding, defender-favouring rewardsR6
Shipping as a four-genre hybridGenre clarity predicts discoverability; novelty carries a measured commercial penaltyOne dominant framing in five seconds, the rest through progressive disclosureR5, R6
Virtual-currency obfuscationA randomised trial shows it inflates spending through money illusion even at 1:1; EU guidance targets itReal-money prices, or a transparent 1:1 rateR2
Strict 50/50 matchmakingChurn rose with stronger opponents; weaker opponents reduced churn more than fair matchesMake the median heist winnableR2
A 44-point touch minimumReal-world error rates only flatten near 9 to 10 mm; edges and corners are worse9 to 10 mm primary controls, away from cornersR3
A complexity budget counting unfamiliar lawsThe limit is interacting elements, not novelty: about fourNever more than four interacting rules at any levelR3
Free chat for minorsMeasured grooming prevalence and off-platform migration riskPreset-phrase chat for the minor cohortR2
Real-time co-op as scopedFull netcode cost for a mode outside the core loopAsynchronous co-op first; real-time only if playtests demand itR4
Teaching the 44 resonances and 12 chordsNobody memorises 56 interactionsSurface them reactively, in playR5
Notifications as a growth leverThree to six pushes a week make about 40% disable themContextual only, low frequency, opt-in requested after value is seenR4
A 5% Workshop publishing targetCreative communities run at roughly 1% creating, 9% editing1.5% publishing, 10% remixing, plus a remix pathR2

Decisions the evidence supports — lock them

DecisionWhat supports it
Server-validated deterministic replayThe strongest anti-cheat posture available, and it doubles as golden-replay regression testing
Cosmetic only, plus a season passAvoids paid randomness and its correlation with problem gambling; removes pay-to-win refund pressure; sidesteps most loot-box regulation. The season pass's shape matches where the industry converged
One-way theftRemoves the victim, which is the cue that would otherwise produce guilt or griefing; and it protects the defender from uncontrollable loss, the purest form of need frustration
Non-violenceViolence adds nothing to enjoyment once competition is controlled for, and the cozy audience is growing and demographically distinct
Foregrounding the absent humanA medium-to-large effect on enjoyment and a large one on arousal, much of it from belief alone
Portrait-first, asynchronous, latency-tolerant coreThumb reach, session shape, and the fact that async needs no netcode at all
Tight scope and a small teamSmall projects succeed around 90% of the time against under 10% for large ones
A crash-free gate of 99.9%Below about 99.82% apps tend to fall under three stars
Six schools and seven realmsBoth sit in the learnable band between Magic and Pokémon
The Workshop as core infrastructureIt is the only credible answer to the content treadmill — provided premise 7 is solved

What only our own playtests can settle

  1. Whether an asynchronous, no-loss heist generates enough tension to be fun. No study covers this loop.
  2. Whether delegated crews feel like playing or watching. Threshold: at least 70% agreeing they felt in control.
  3. Whether players build defences at all, and at what rate.
  4. Whether the store page communicates the game in five seconds.
  5. Whether the vocabulary clears a 70% post-tutorial comprehension bar.
  6. Whether eight notes is one too many for a day-one mental model.
  7. Whether the 144-form collection sustains a chase, and where it drops off.
  8. Whether the heist clock is a pleasure or a stressor.
  9. Whether portrait or landscape is chosen when both are one tap away.
  10. Whether the Island Fund crowds out the creators it is meant to reward.
  11. Our own estimation error and our own AI speedup.
  12. The sustainable content cadence, measured as consumption against production.

The risk register, ranked

RankRiskWhy it ranks hereMain mitigation
1Nobody builds defencesBreaks the content ecosystem, the Workshop and the human-presence loop at onceMandatory light build, seeding, defender-favouring rewards, 15 to 20% first-week publishing benchmark
2Production and executionBase-rate failure plus the planning fallacy plus the AI calibration illusion; a small team cannot hire its way outScope discipline, reference-class forecasting, no crunch
3The concept does not communicateNovelty carries a measured penalty and the game fits no clean genre tagAnchored differentiation, show-don't-tell store page, five-second comprehension test
4Cold startAsync raiding, a Workshop and clans all need critical mass to be funEcho universes, seeded islands, soft launch in few markets
5Content treadmillShipping is likely; sustaining is the hard partThe Workshop, cadence set from measured capacity
6Trust and safety at scaleUser-made content plus chat plus clans in twelve languages, with minors presentPreset chat for minors, hash-matching, human review, DSA-compliant reporting
7Complexity overwhelms new playersThe four-rule limit against 48 laws and 56 combinationsStaged unlocks, reactive surfacing, one new term per beat
8Device and performance realityLow-end Android across twelve marketsMid-range reference device, crash and ANR gates, small install size
9Revenue insufficiencyCosmetic-only earns less per player by designDeliberate trade; retention and reach must carry it

30.9 Where the reviews disagree

Six reviews commissioned separately do not produce one voice. The tensions matter more than the agreements.

TensionThe two sidesResolution
LatencyHuman factors says responsiveness is critical (11 ms for drag). Operations says network latency barely matters for an asynchronous loopBoth are right about different things. Spend on local input and feedback timing; spend nothing on network latency — unless real-time co-op is built, when both costs arrive at once
NotificationsFulfilment research is wary of extrinsic nudges. Growth thinking wants notifications to drive returnsThe evidence resolves it in fulfilment's favour: contextual notifications about real events beat generic engagement blasts, which actively cause uninstalls
Content velocityLive-ops says cadence sustains retention. Production says crunching to hit cadence raises defects and burns out a small teamThe Workshop, plus a cadence derived from measured capacity, and no public roadmap that requires crunch
Playtest methodsHuman factors and playtest methodology value small-N qualitative work. Telemetry values large-N behaviourFive to eight users for usability, in three rounds; live behaviour for fun, balance and retention. Do not ask five testers a question only fifty thousand players can answer
Humanising the defenderPremise 1 says make the absent opponent feel human, because that is where the emotional charge lives. Premise 5 says the more human they feel, the more taking from them could feel wrongOne-way theft is what makes both possible at once: enough humanity to feel real, not enough harm to feel cruel. This is the single most elegant interaction between reviews — and it needs a playtest
DifficultyEarlier engagement research said choice, novelty and suspense beat difficulty tuning. Matchmaking research says target win rates slightly above evenNot in conflict: let players choose difficulty openly, and set the default target pool so the median run is winnable
Creator paymentFulfilment research says money crowds out the most motivated creators. The business case says unpaid creator economies age badlyTaken knowingly: a fixed fund, paid in arrears with no published rate, capped to favour the tail, with a stated failure condition

30.10 The measurement plan that falls out of all six

What to measureInstrumentThreshold that forces a change
Needs met and needs frustratedBANGS — measures both directionsFrustration rising in a cohort, even with satisfaction flat
Experience across eleven constructsPXI, or the eleven-item miniPXI liveMastery, curiosity, autonomy, control or goals below +1.5; anything below 0
Meaning, separately from funThe three-item appreciation scaleTests the endgame hypothesis directly
Harmonious against obsessive playThe Passion ScalePlaytime up while enjoyment and energy fall — the mechanic goes
Kind of challengeCORGISCognitive and decision-making below the midpoint, or performative above it
BelongingInvestment Model Scale; the closeness pictogramInvestment high but satisfaction low — players are trapped, not committed
Whether it was worth itOne tap after each sessionBelow 4.3 out of 5
Early churnRecency of absence, plus the funnelTriggers a legacy card, never a win-back campaign
StabilityCrash-free sessions, ANR rateBelow 99.9%, or ANR above 0.47%
Economy healthPrice index, coefficient of variation, wealth concentrationSustained inflation or a rising Gini among veterans
The Island FundOutput and meaning among the top 200 creators, before and six months afterEither falling — the fund is withdrawn

30.11 What this research cannot tell us

  • Whether Ruleborn is fun. Research rules out bad ideas and sets priors. It cannot confirm that a specific game is enjoyable. Only the vertical slice can, against the gate: seven of ten outside testers asking to play again.
  • Whether one-way theft carries tension. No study covers a loop where the defender loses nothing. This is the most important untested thing in the design.
  • Whether people will design defences. The evidence says probably not by default; it cannot say whether our specific mitigations work.
  • How to rate a player-built island's difficulty. The matchmaking literature is almost entirely live player-versus-player.
  • Whether preset chat is safer than filtered chat for minors. No direct comparison exists; we follow safety-by-design inference.
  • What localisation returns per language for a strategy game. Industry figures only, with undisclosed methods.
  • Which accessibility features move retention. The guidelines are endorsed but not experimentally validated.
  • Our own numbers. Every count in the game — 48 laws, 8 notes, 144 forms, a 150 to 240 second clock — sits inside a plausible range the literature can bound but not fix.
The honest summary

Six reviews and roughly 200 sources have produced a design that is unusually well grounded for its stage, and a clear-eyed list of the four or five things most likely to kill it. What they have not produced, and cannot, is evidence that the game is good. That comes from a playable heist and ten strangers.

30.12 Review 7 — Evidence gathering and minimum-cost operations

A seventh review was commissioned once the design was stable, to answer two questions the others had left open: how to gather primary evidence about this game rather than about games in general, and how to run it for as little money as possible given that development labour is free but every recurring bill is not.

FindingWhat it changed
The asynchronous, deterministic design avoids the two costs that dominate live games: egress and positional telemetry. Storage with no egress fee and per-request compute make the realistic bill roughly nothing at a thousand players, tens of dollars at ten thousand, and low hundreds at a hundred thousandThe stack and the cost table in 24.1
Because replays can be re-simulated, route and detection heatmaps can be regenerated server-side without the client ever sending coordinatesFree spatial analytics (24.3)
All of it depends on the simulation being bit-identical across processors, which floating-point arithmetic does not guaranteeFixed-point maths, and the determinism spike as the first task in the project (24.2, 26.7)
Hosting player-uploaded images creates a legal duty to detect child sexual abuse material, and the tooling is priced for platforms rather than individualsWorkshop islands are structured data only; no image uploads, ever (18.6, 20.10)
In-app surveys answer at about 13%, and about 19% in entertainment apps; self-reported and logged play time diverge systematicallyThe measurement plan in 25.5, and the rule that behaviour wins on fact while self-report wins on interpretation
Both stores halve commission below a million dollars a year, act as seller of record for VAT, and handle withholding through a treaty formThe business model in 22.5
The unavoidable cash costs are small and mostly legal: store fees, a trade mark, an accountant, translation upkeepThe checklist in 26.6 and the order of work in 26.7

30.13 Review 8 — Driving the cost to nothing

An eighth review asked how close to free this game can be run at a million monthly players, under three constraints the developer set: no machine learning anywhere, no trade mark registration, and nothing licensed or paid for.

FindingWhat it changed
The design's own properties — structured data, seeds and input logs, no uploads, preset phrases — put its whole traffic profile inside permanent free tiers. About 100 to 200 kilobytes per player per day means under a terabyte and a half a month at a million players, on storage that charges nothing for bandwidthThe architecture and cost table in 24.1, and the byte budget in 24.4
Most of the game can be delivered as immutable files, because an opponent is a snapshot rather than a person. Only publishing, validation, league tables and clan state need a machine that thinks, and those are write-lightStatic-first delivery, with serverless functions behind it (24.4, 24.6)
The only unavoidable recurring cost is the Apple developer programme at $99 a year. Google is $25 once, a domain is optional, and the privacy policy is free to write and hostThe irreducible cost in 24.5 and the model in 22.5
Preset-phrase chat removes the need for any moderation classifier, which is the only place this game would otherwise have used machine learningDeterministic moderation confirmed as the design, not a compromise (20.10)
Not registering a trade mark is a real but bounded risk: unregistered rights exist in the market of actual use, both stores reserve names first-come, and both run disputes without requiring a registrationThe position and its mitigations in 26.6
Public-domain and permissive licences are genuinely free; attribution chains, share-alike, non-commercial terms, "royalty-free" stock and desktop-only fonts are not. Generating the world in code avoids the question entirelyMade, not licensed (21.11)

30.14 Review 9 — Code architecture and the build plan

A ninth review answered two engineering questions: how to build this so the same simulation runs on a phone and inside a server function, and how much work that actually is when the work is done by a coding agent.

FindingWhat it changed
The simulation must be written once and compiled twice — into the app and to WebAssembly — because two implementations would eventually disagree, and that disagreement is the one failure the whole design cannot absorbThe Rust core in 24.7, and the engine row in 24
Floating point cannot be made identical across processors, since transcendental functions are library-dependent. Fixed point, integer trigonometry and integer randomness are the standard answer in games that replay or lockstepThe number rules in 24.7
A native extension is linked into the signed application at build time, so it is not downloaded code under the store rules. A runtime WebAssembly loader on the device would beRecorded as a hard constraint (24.7)
Rust extensions on mobile are officially experimental, with no confirmed commercial mobile game shipped on them. This is the thinnest part of the whole architectureThe spike gate and the C# fallback trigger (24.2, 24.7)
Re-simulating every heist would exceed the per-request compute budget for no security gainSampled validation, corrected from the earlier "validate everything" rule (24)
Agent-built codebases fail by writing tests that pass rather than tests that test — one study found a suite fully green while most modules ended up imported by nothingHand-written golden fixtures and behaviour-asserting tests the agent cannot satisfy by cheating (24.9)
Reliable autonomous completion tops out well below maximum capability: around half an hour of human-equivalent work, even where far longer tasks can be attemptedThe run calibration and the roadmap in 26.8

30.15 Review 10 — Raids, rarity and defence

A tenth review examined three weaknesses raised in design review: whether a raid has a real purpose, whether rarity can be finer without becoming power, and whether anything but laws actually defends a universe.

FindingWhat it changed
Bottleneck resources do drive a core loop, but the resented version is the one that decides when a player may pursue what they want. The admired version is always available and directional by the player's own goalPages lean toward the school raided, with no clock gating (7.6)
The proposal was wrong in one place: making pages obtainable only by raiding would punish the large share of players who prefer building, which an earlier review identified as the riskiest assumption in the designA slow Library trickle at home, with raiding worth two to three sessions of it. Primary, not sole
Rarity is properly a dial for complexity, effect size and excitement rather than power — but no shipped competitive game has fully separated the two, so something else must do the balancingFive ranks, and scouting visibility charged against strength as the primary offset (7.10)
Conditional, build-around power is enjoyed; flat drawbacks are resentedRare laws are powerful when a condition you control is met, rather than costly to own
Sets of seven to twelve are where people push to finish; 48 reads as endlessCollection goals grouped by school, eight each
No single element stops an attack in the base builders this borrows from: walls funnel, traps punish the route, and held-back defenders are the hidden win conditionFive layers of comparable weight, none above a quarter (13)
Because theft here is one-way and painless, this game can afford a much higher defence-hold rate than a punishing base builder — and should, because that is what makes designing worth doingThe fairness targets in 13.2, and the rule that the shape of outcomes matters more than the average

30.16 Review 11 — The four specifications and the three gates

An eleventh review answered the two questions that stood between the design and a first line of code: what exactly to build, and what to prove before building it.

FindingWhat it changed
Shipped stealth games use nested vision zones rather than one cone, a gradual meter rather than a binary, and sound that travels along paths rather than through wallsThe whole of 12.17, previously the least specified system in the document
For a top-down game that shows its cones, the readable choice is full determinism: no probability in detection at allA design rule as much as a technical one, and required anyway by server re-simulation
Modifier systems that must agree forever need a fixed resolution order, not an arbitrary oneThe four-step order in 8.7, and paradoxes written as "cannot" rather than "less"
Thirty ticks a second, commands rather than state, a checksum every tick and one kept per secondThe contract in 24.10, and the confirmation that a heist fits in under two kilobytes
Replays stay valid across patches only if they record the rules they were played underPin-don't-patch, and the grace state for islands that a re-tune pushes over budget (24.11)
Tension does not require loss: near-misses raise arousal even when nothing is lost, and more so when the player chose the actionThe first gate, and confidence that one-way theft is not a design flaw
Stated willingness to create is close to worthless — the gap between intending and doing runs at about 46%The forced-then-free test and the three-way decision in 13.3
Rust on mobile is experimental, with no shipped title found and the iOS issue still openThe spike as a gate, and a fallback ladder decided in advance rather than in a panic (24.7)

30.17 Review 12 — The three blockers

A twelfth review answered the three things that stood between a finished design and a first line of code: what a raid pays, what a defence may hold and how its layers are measured, and what happens when the network is not there.

FindingWhat it changed
The base builders pay a percentage of what the defender holds — but in those games the loot leaves the defender. Here it is created, so copying them would tie the inflation rate to hoardingThe haul is driven by the raider's own level, with the target's wealth clamped to a narrow band (9.6)
One shipped game already has the sealed-vault pattern, including a guarantee that a raider never leaves with nothingThe floor on the richness term, so a fully sealed island still pays
An uncapped faucet collapses a currency, and the controls are caps, decay and diminishing returns — especially where there is no hard-currency sink, as herePer-raid, daily and weekly caps, with weekly set at five days rather than seven
Base builders pace progression through slot limits per level, not through cost aloneThe budget table in 13.4, where limits rather than prices enforce the quarter ceiling
Attributing an outcome among contributing parts is a solved problem with a standard method, already used to attribute win rates in a live game. With five layers there are only 32 combinations, so it can be computed exactly rather than approximatedA layer's share becomes measurable: switch it off, re-run, divide the credit (13.4)
Idempotency keys derived from the business fields are the standard way to make a submission exactly-once across retriesThe offline queue and the guarantee that a haul cannot be paid twice (24.12)
Device clocks cannot be trusted in a game with cooldowns and seasonsThe server clock as the only clock
Content made by a deleted account is not personal data once the name is severed; a banned account is different, and the law permits keeping the minimum needed to enforce itThe policy in 20.12, including publishing and storage limits
